2	---
3	title: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome in Overhead Throwing Athletes — Evidence Brief
4	date: 2026-09-18
5	author: Eric Rash (Applied Performance, Baylor Athletics)
6	purpose: Evidence brief for softball strength & conditioning staff on TOS causes, risk factors, and mitigation
7	status: complete
8	tags: [sport-science, softball, baseball, thoracic-outlet-syndrome, overhead-athlete, injury-risk, workload]
9	---
10	
11	# Thoracic Outlet Syndrome in Overhead Throwing Athletes
12	
13	**An evidence brief for softball performance staff.**
14	
15	Prepared 2026-09-18. Every citation in this document was verified against PubMed
16	(NCBI E-utilities), Europe PMC, or the publisher record before inclusion.
17	Sources from the Applied Performance Zotero library are marked
18	`[Zotero: KEY, p. N]`. All others are marked `[External]` and are peer-reviewed
19	primary sources or systematic reviews unless stated otherwise.
20	
21	> **How to read the confidence labels.** This brief separates what is
22	> **Established** (measured, replicated), **Plausible but unproven** (a coherent
23	> mechanism with no direct test), and **Speculation** (asserted in practice,
24	> unsupported in literature). The distinction matters. A claim presented as
25	> stronger than it is will not survive a second opinion, and it will cost the
26	> person making it credibility on the claims that *are* solid.
27	
28	---
29	
30	## Bottom line up front
31	
32	1. **The peer comparison cannot be made.** TOS is not separately coded in the
33	   NCAA Injury Surveillance Program. There is no national softball TOS rate to
34	   compare against. (§1.4)
35	2. **TOS is rare enough that no single program can estimate its own rate.**
36	   Population incidence is roughly **2–3 per 100,000 per year** for neurogenic
37	   TOS. On a 35-athlete roster, expected cases per season is about **0.0014**.
38	   Two cases is a plausible chance cluster, not a signal. (§1.5)
39	3. **Diagnosis drives counts at least as much as biology does.** There is no
40	   gold-standard test for neurogenic TOS. The provocative test most used in an
41	   athletic training room is **positive in 47–62% of people who do not have
42	   TOS**. A program that starts looking will find cases; one that does not,
43	   will not. (§1.3)
44	4. **The throwing motion is the exposure, and the histology does not implicate
45	   the weight room.** The cocked position roughly doubles scalene stiffness. The
46	   scalene muscle changes found in TOS patients are type II *atrophy* plus
47	   fibrosis — the opposite of a resistance-training signature. (§2.4, §2.5)
48	5. **"Don't lift before throwing" has no research support**, and the adjacent
49	   evidence leans against it. The defensible version is much narrower. (§4)
50	6. **The endurance hypothesis is coherent and worth acting on, but it is not
51	   established.** The best supporting study found a 45% rotator endurance
52	   deficit in TOS patients — in 40-year-old non-athletes, with the direction of
53	   causation unresolved. (§3)
54	7. **The strongest modifiable exposure is workload, and it is not the strength
55	   coach's lever.** Collegiate softball pitchers throw **2.9× the innings of
56	   baseball pitchers on a staff one-third the size**, under no pitch count limit
57	   and no mandated rest — and about **half of true pitch volume is bullpen and
58	   warm-up that nobody counts**. (§5)
59	
60	---
61	
62	## Section 1 — What TOS is, how common it is, and why the peer comparison fails
63	
64	### 1.1 Three conditions, not one
65	
66	TOS is compression of the brachial plexus, subclavian artery, or subclavian vein
67	in one of three anatomical spaces. The subtypes behave very differently and
68	should never be discussed as a single entity.
69	
70	| Subtype | General population | Athletes |
71	|---|---|---|
72	| **Neurogenic (nTOS)** | 82–95% | 66–74% |
73	| **Venous (vTOS / Paget-Schroetter, effort thrombosis)** | 3–16% | **26–34%** |
74	| **Arterial (aTOS)** | ~1–2% | ~2% (1 of 52 in the largest pro series) |
75	
76	`[External]` Illig KA, et al. *Ann Vasc Surg* 2021;70:263-72. PMID 32771464 — 526 consecutive referrals: 82% nTOS, 16% vTOS, 2% aTOS.
77	`[External]` Chandra V, Little C, Lee JT. *J Vasc Surg* 2014;60(4):1012-7. PMID 24835692 — 41 competitive athletes: 66% nTOS, 34% Paget-Schroetter.
78	`[External]` Chauhan A, et al. *Am J Sports Med* 2024;52(7):1692-9. PMID 38702964 — 52 pro baseball players: 69% neurogenic, 29% venous.
79	`[External]` Gutman MJ, et al. *Phys Sportsmed* 2022;50(2):141-6. PMID 33472488 — 27 MLB pitchers: 74% nTOS, 26% vTOS.
80	
81	**Established.** Venous TOS is roughly **5- to 10-fold over-represented in
82	athletes** relative to the general population. The mechanism is chronic
83	repetitive compression of the subclavian vein in the costoclavicular space.
84	`[External]` Vemuri C, et al. *J Vasc Surg Venous Lymphat Disord* 2016;4(4):485-500. PMID 27639006.
85	
86	**Caveat:** every athlete proportion above is a *referral-center or treated-case*
87	proportion, not an incidence. They describe the mix among athletes who reached a
88	TOS surgeon — not the mix among athletes who have TOS.
89	
90	### 1.2 The base rate — and a statistic to stop repeating
91	
92	**Do not use "3–80 per 1,000."** It is the most commonly cited TOS incidence
93	figure and it does not survive tracing:
94	
95	1. StatPearls (where most clinicians land) says "3 to 80 cases per 1,000," citing —
96	2. Jones MR, et al. *Pain Ther* 2019;8(1):5-18 (PMID 31037504), which says
97	   "Several articles report an incidence of 3–80/1000 [4]," citing —
98	3. Citisli V. *J Pain Relief* 2015;4(2):1-7 — **which is not indexed in
99	   PubMed/MEDLINE at all.** A PubMed author search returns zero results.
100	
101	A 27-fold-wide range is itself the tell that nobody measured anything.
102	
103	**What the actual data say.** `[External]` Illig KA, Rodriguez-Zoppi E.
104	*Thorac Surg Clin* 2021;31(1):11-17. PMID 33220767, opening line: *"The incidence
105	of neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome is completely unknown, and has been wildly
106	overestimated in the past."* Their prospective referral database back-calculates:
107	
108	- **nTOS ≈ 2–3 per 100,000 per year**
109	- **vTOS ≈ 0.5–1 per 100,000 per year**
110	- **aTOS sporadic**
111	
112	The discrepancy between the folklore figure and the measured one is **100-fold
113	to 2,700-fold**.
114	
115	### 1.3 There is no gold-standard test — and the field says so in its own documents
116	
117	**Established, and this is the most defensible section of the brief.**
118	
119	- The **SVS reporting standards** define nTOS as ≥3 of 4 criteria, one of which
120	  is *absence of other pathology explaining the symptoms* (a diagnosis of
121	  exclusion) and one of which is *response to a scalene block* (a therapeutic
122	  trial, not a test). No imaging, electrodiagnostic, or laboratory criterion
123	  exists. `[External]` Illig KA, et al. *J Vasc Surg* 2016;64(3):e23-35. PMID 27565607.
124	- `[External]` Sanders RJ, Hammond SL, Rao NM. *Neurologist* 2008;14(6):365-73. PMID 19008742:
125	  *"there is no standard objective test to confirm clinical impressions... To
126	  date there is still no reliable objective test to confirm the diagnosis."*
127	- **Cochrane:** *"TOS is one of the most controversial diagnoses in clinical
128	  medicine."* The review *"had to rely exclusively on the diagnosis of TOS by the
129	  investigators in the reviewed studies."* Only **two RCTs worldwide** met a
130	  6-month follow-up bar. `[External]` Povlsen B, Hansson T, Povlsen SD. *Cochrane Database Syst Rev* 2014;(11):CD007218. PMID 25427003.
131	- **Wilbourn vs Roos, *Muscle Nerve* 1999** — "TOS is overdiagnosed" and "TOS is
132	  underdiagnosed," published back to back in the same issue of the same journal.
133	  `[External]` PMID 9883870 / PMID 9883869.
134	- Even at a **dedicated TOS center**, only **150 of 183 (82%)** of new nTOS
135	  referrals met an established criteria set. `[External]` Balderman J, et al. *J Vasc Surg* 2017;66(2):533-544.e2. PMID 28735950.
136	- A Delphi expert consensus published in 2026 — a decade after the SVS standards —
137	  exists precisely because criteria remain unsettled. **Its fifth criterion is
138	  "participation in work/exercise requiring repetitive arm stress (overhead
139	  athletes, throwing sports)."** `[External]` Wagner ER, et al. *Orthop J Sports Med* 2026;14(5):23259671261440925. PMID 42169800.
140	
141	  **Read that last one twice.** Being an overhead athlete is itself a formal
142	  diagnostic criterion for nTOS. For a program comparing its softball TOS rate
143	  to peers, that is circular: athlete status is an *input* to the diagnosis.
144	
145	**False-positive rates of provocative tests in people who do not have TOS:**
146	
147	| Test | Rayan 1995 (200 asymptomatic limbs) | Plewa 1998 (53 healthy) | Nord 2008 (normals) |
148	|---|---|---|---|
149	| Adson's | 13.5% vascular / 2% neuro | 11% pulse | 9–20% |
150	| Costoclavicular | 47% vascular / 10% neuro | 11% pulse / 15% paresthesia | 16% |
151	| Wright's / hyperabduction | **57% vascular** / 16.5% neuro | — | — |
152	| **Roos / EAST** | — | **62% pulse, 36% paresthesia, 21% pain** | **47%** |
153	| **≥1 test positive** | — | — | **56% of normals** |
154	
155	`[External]` Rayan GM, Jensen C. *J Shoulder Elbow Surg* 1995;4(2):113-7. PMID 7600161.
156	`[External]` Plewa MC, Delinger M. *Acad Emerg Med* 1998;5(4):337-42. PMID 9562199.
157	`[External]` Nord KM, et al. *Electromyogr Clin Neurophysiol* 2008;48(2):67-74. PMID 18435210.
158	`[External]` Warrens AN, Heaton JM. *Ann R Coll Surg Engl* 1987;69(5):203-4. PMID 3674682 — 58% of volunteers positive on ≥1 maneuver, in a group where only 17% had any symptoms.
159	
160	Nord 2008 adds the decisive number: in **carpal tunnel patients** — who by
161	definition do not have TOS — Roos/EAST was positive in **77%**, and **94% had at
162	least one positive TOS maneuver.** Gillard 2001 reduces it to one figure:
163	provocative tests have **mean specificity 53%**. `[External]` Gillard J, et al. *Joint Bone Spine* 2001;68(5):416-24. PMID 11707008.
164	
165	**Practical implication.** The Roos/EAST test — the one most likely to be used in
166	an athletic training room — is positive in roughly **half of people who do not
167	have TOS**. Screening a 35-athlete roster with EAST would be expected to flag
168	16–20 healthy athletes.
169	
170	### 1.4 TOS is not coded in the NCAA ISP — the peer comparison cannot be made
171	
172	**Established.**
173	
174	- The ISP data model releases **body part or system affected**, **specific
175	  injury**, and **type of injury**. The body-part list is coarse and anatomical:
176	  head/face, neck, shoulder, arm or elbow, hand/wrist, trunk, hip/groin, thigh,
177	  knee, lower leg, ankle, foot, other. **There is no "thoracic outlet" site and
178	  no vascular or peripheral-nerve category.** `[External]` Kerr ZY, et al. *J Athl Train* 2014;49(4):552-60. PMID 24870292.
179	- The diagnosis taxonomy is **injury-type** based — strains, sprains, contusions,
180	  inflammatory conditions, concussion — not disease-entity based.
181	- **TOS appears nowhere** in the two most recent 5-year NCAA baseball and
182	  softball epidemiology reports, or in the decade-long report.
183	  `[External]` Boltz AJ, et al. *J Athl Train* 2021;56(7):742-9. PMID 34280265. / Veillard KL, et al. *J Athl Train* 2021;56(7):734-41. PMID 34280289. / Wasserman EB, et al. *J Athl Train* 2019;54(2):198-211. PMID 30951387.
184	- The ISP denominator is **athlete-exposures, not athletes or rosters**, drawn
185	  from a **convenience sample** — an annual average of ~34 collegiate baseball
186	  teams — which the authors themselves warn "should be interpreted with caution."
187	
188	**Honest limit:** the Datalys ISP documentation page returned HTTP 404, so I
189	cannot prove no internal code string exists. What is demonstrable: TOS is not
190	*reported* in any published NCAA ISP baseball or softball output and is not in
191	the released taxonomies. A program wanting certainty should submit a data
192	request to the Datalys Center.
193	
194	**The one usable collegiate denominator** comes from a chart review, not the ISP:
195	`[External]` Talutis SD, et al. *J Vasc Surg* 2025;82(1):155-62. PMID 40132734 —
196	**15,609 NCAA Division I athletes, 21 sports, 7 years, 76 TOS cases (0.48%).**
197	
198	| Sport | TOS prevalence |
199	|---|---|
200	| Tennis | 2.6% |
201	| **Softball** | **1.3%** |
202	| Rowing | 1.3% |
203	| All sports | 0.48% |
204	
205	90.8% neurogenic, 9.2% venous. **96.0% managed without surgery; 95.4% returned
206	to unrestricted competition.** Softball sits above the all-sport baseline but
207	below tennis — and the outcomes are good.
208	
209	### 1.5 Why a roster-level comparison is statistically meaningless
210	
211	Using Illig's estimate of roughly 4 per 100,000 per year for all TOS combined, a
212	35-athlete roster observed for one season has an expected count of **0.0014
213	cases**.
214	
215	- **Zero cases tells you nothing.** By the rule of three, 35 athlete-years with
216	  zero events puts the 95% upper bound at 3/35 ≈ **8.6% per athlete-season** —
217	  four orders of magnitude above the true rate. A program with no cases has no
218	  evidence it is below average. `[External]` Hanley JA, Lippman-Hand A. *JAMA* 1983;249(13):1743-5. PMID 6827763.
219	- **One case looks catastrophic and means almost nothing.** The exact Poisson 95%
220	  CI on a single observed event is (0.03, 5.6) events. The interval admits
221	  essentially any hypothesis.
222	- **Two cases is a plausible chance cluster.** Poisson 95% CI on 2 events:
223	  (0.24, 7.2). A peer program with 0 and a peer program with 3 are not
224	  statistically distinguishable at these counts.
225	- **Ascertainment dominates everything.** 56% of normals screen positive on at
226	  least one provocative maneuver, and being an overhead athlete is a formal
227	  diagnostic criterion. Any observed between-program difference is far more
228	  likely to measure the **referral pathway** — whether the school has a
229	  relationship with a TOS center — than the underlying biology.
230	
231	**The framing to take into the room:** TOS is rare enough that no single athletic
232	program generates a sample large enough to estimate its own rate, let alone
233	compare it to a peer's. The meaningful question is not *"is our rate high?"* but
234	*"is our diagnostic and referral pathway appropriate, and are our modifiable
235	exposures managed?"*
236	
237	### 1.6 Outcomes, for reassurance
238	
239	Five independent professional-baseball return-to-play studies exist, and they
240	converge tightly: **74–81% return to play at 9–11 months.**
241	
242	| Study | n | RTP | Performance conclusion |
243	|---|---|---|---|
244	| Thompson 2017 | 13 MLB pitchers | 77% at 10.8 mo | 75% of 72 PitchF/x metrics unchanged; max velocity −0.6 mph (P=.047) |
245	| Gutman 2022 | 27 MLB pitchers | 74% at 297 d | ERA worse (3.66→4.50, P=.03); velocity unchanged |
246	| Arnold 2022 | 26 MLB pitchers | 81% at 10 mo | No difference vs matched controls |
247	| **Chauhan 2024** | 52 pro (88% pitchers) | **79% at 9.5 mo** | **Declines present, but no faster than matched healthy controls aging normally** |
248	
249	`[External]` Thompson RW, et al. *Ann Vasc Surg* 2017;39:216-27. PMID 27522980. / Gutman MJ, et al. PMID 33472488. / Arnold MT, et al. *Orthop J Sports Med* 2022;10(4):23259671221079835. PMID 35494495. / Chauhan A, et al. PMID 38702964.
250	
251	**The narrative that TOS surgery collapses a pitcher's career is supported by
252	exactly one study** (Gutman's unmatched pre/post ERA comparison) **and
253	contradicted by the two that used matched controls.** Chauhan 2024 — the only one
254	using MLB's internal Health and Injury Tracking System rather than press reports —
255	concluded the decline after TOS surgery was no faster than in healthy pitchers
256	aging normally. An unmatched pre/post design on a cohort with mean age ~29–30
257	will manufacture a decline out of ordinary aging.
258	
259	Funakoshi 2024, the largest overhead-athlete series (79 athletes: **baseball 67,
260	tennis 4, softball 3, volleyball 3, swimming 1, handball 1**), reported **97%
261	return to play and 81% return to the same level** at 7.3 ± 5.1 months, with
262	**91.1% excellent/good** Roos scores in athletes vs 62.8% in non-athletes.
263	`[External]` Funakoshi T, et al. *JSES Int* 2024;8(3):620-9. PMID 38707577.
264	
265	---
266	
267	## Section 2 — What actually causes TOS in throwing athletes
268	
269	### 2.1 The three compression spaces
270	
271	**Established.**
272	
273	| Space | Boundaries | Contents |
274	|---|---|---|
275	| **Interscalene triangle** | Anterior scalene (front), middle scalene (back), first rib (below) | Brachial plexus **trunks**, subclavian **artery**. The subclavian vein passes *anterior* to the anterior scalene and is not in this triangle. |
276	| **Costoclavicular space** | Clavicle and subclavius (above), first rib (below) | Plexus **divisions**, subclavian artery **and vein** |
277	| **Subcoracoid / retropectoralis minor space** | Pectoralis minor and its coracoid insertion (front), chest wall (behind) | Plexus **cords**, axillary artery and vein |
278	
279	For **arterial** compression the costoclavicular space is the discriminating
280	site. Demondion 2006 imaged 44 volunteers and 28 arterial-TOS patients at 0°,
281	90°, 130° and 170° abduction: no significant arterial stenosis in the
282	interscalene triangle or retropectoralis minor space in either group; only the
283	costoclavicular space separated patients from volunteers, at every angle, with
284	**130° hyperabduction most discriminating**. `[External]` Demondion X, et al. *J Ultrasound Med* 2006;25(2):217-24. PMID 16439785.
285	
286	The common claim that the **subcoracoid space is the space most implicated in
287	throwers** is **plausible but unproven** — no study compares the three spaces
288	head-to-head in throwing athletes. It rests on a general surgical population
289	(>75% of nTOS patients also had pectoralis minor syndrome; ~30% had it alone)
290	plus expert opinion. `[External]` Sanders RJ, Rao NM. *Ann Vasc Surg* 2010;24(6):701-8. PMID 20471786.
291	
292	### 2.2 Structural predisposition — common, and usually silent
293	
294	**Established.**
295	
296	- **Cervical rib: 0.74%** of 1,352 London chest radiographs (females 1.09%,
297	  males 0.42%); corroborated at **0.7%** in 6,571 Nigerian radiographs.
298	  `[External]` Brewin J, Hill M, Ellis H. *Clin Anat* 2009;22(3):331-6. PMID 19280652. / Ezeofor SN, et al. *Niger J Clin Pract* 2016;19(4):513-6. PMID 27251970.
299	- **Elongated C7 transverse process: 2.21%** — about three times more common than
300	  a cervical rib, and the more likely bony contributor in any given athlete.
301	- **Fibromuscular bands.** Roos described **seven** types in 1976 and **nine** by
302	  1980 across 1,120 operations. **One third of 58 cadaver thoracic outlets showed
303	  at least one** — in people who never had symptoms. `[External]` Roos DB. *Am J Surg* 1976;132(6):771-8. PMID 998867. / *Acta Chir Belg* 1980;79(5):353-61. PMID 7223264.
304	  - *The frequently cited "Roos described 14 types" appears in no Roos primary
305	    source. Cite nine (1980). Do not repeat the 14 figure.*
306	- **Scalene anatomy is highly variable.** The textbook arrangement — plexus
307	  passing between anterior and middle scalene — was present in **only 60%** of 51
308	  cadavers. `[External]` Harry WG, Bennett JD, Guha SC. *Clin Anat* 1997;10(4):250-2. PMID 9213042.
309	- **In TOS surgical series anomalies are the norm:** 66% of 200 consecutive cases
310	  had developmental abnormalities — 20 supernumerary scalenes, 86 scalene and 39
311	  subclavius variations. `[External]` Makhoul RG, Machleder HI. *J Vasc Surg* 1992;16(4):534-42. PMID 1404675.
312	
313	**The honest caveat, and it matters.** Predisposition is not causation. Roos
314	found his bands in a third of *asymptomatic* cadavers. Makhoul & Machleder
315	concluded morphology alone predicted the clinical syndrome *only* for
316	Paget-Schroetter. The defensible framing is: **structural narrowing is common,
317	usually silent, and becomes symptomatic when loaded.** That makes TOS a screening
318	and load-management problem — not an act of God, and not an exoneration.
319	
320	### 2.3 First rib stress fracture — a throwing injury inside the outlet
321	
322	**Established.** 24 first-rib stress fractures in overhead throwing athletes,
323	mean age 16.8 years, dominant arm, presenting as posterior shoulder pain on
324	throwing — and "some patients may have symptoms consistent with thoracic outlet
325	syndrome." `[External]` Funakoshi T, et al. *J Bone Joint Surg Am* 2019;101(10):896-903. PMID 31094981.
326	
327	Callus after such a fracture has caused frank arterial TOS with cerebellar
328	infarction in a baseball player. `[External]` Suehara Y, et al. *JBJS Case Connect* 2017;7(3):e64. PMID 29252893.
329	
330	A 2025 case in a 12-year-old elite pitcher fractured at the **serratus anterior
331	attachment** and presented as scapular winging and snapping — i.e. a first-rib
332	stress fracture can masquerade as exactly the scapular control problem a strength
333	coach would be asked to fix. `[External]` Yoon Y, et al. *Diagnostics (Basel)* 2025;15(19):2437. PMID 41095656.
334	
335	### 2.4 The scalene histology — why the weight room is the wrong suspect
336	
337	**Established, and the single most useful finding in this brief.**
338	
339	Two independent biopsy series of scalene muscles taken at surgery from TOS
340	patients found the same pattern:
341	
342	| Finding | Machleder 1986 | Sanders 1990 |
343	|---|---|---|
344	| Type I (slow/tonic) fiber predominance | **85.1% ± 5.1%** | **78% vs 53%** in controls |
345	| Type II fibers | — | **Atrophied** |
346	| Connective tissue (fibrosis) | — | **36% vs <15%** in controls |
347	
348	`[External]` Machleder HI, Moll F, Verity MA. *Arch Surg* 1986;121(10):1141-4. PMID 3767646.
349	`[External]` Sanders RJ, Jackson CG, Banchero N, Pearce WH. *Am J Surg* 1990;159(2):231-6. PMID 2301718.
350	
351	Machleder's interpretation: the anterior scalene "demonstrates an extraordinary
352	adaptive transformation and recruitment response in the type 1 fiber system
353	reflecting chronic increased tone or motor neuron stimulation."
354	
355	**Why this matters.** Resistance training produces **type II hypertrophy**. The
356	scalene muscle in TOS shows **type II atrophy plus fibrosis and type I
357	predominance**. That is the signature of chronic sustained tone and of injury —
358	not of a training adaptation. If anyone argues that weight-room hypertrophy built
359	the compressing muscle, the histology does not support it.
360	
361	Treat the *pattern* as established and the *exact percentages* as study-specific;
362	both are surgical biopsy series with convenience controls.
363	
364	### 2.5 Throwing loads the outlet — measurably
365	
366	**Established.** Shear wave elastography on 30 collegiate baseball pitchers:
367	
368	| Position | Anterior scalene | Middle scalene |
369	|---|---|---|
370	| Neutral | 9.4 ± 2.0 kPa | 10.9 ± 3.4 kPa |
371	| **ABER (cocked)** | **14.4 ± 3.8 kPa** (P<.001) | **15.8 ± 5.0 kPa** (P<.001) |
372	| ABER + neck rotation away | **18.1 ± 4.6 kPa** | 15.8 ± 2.6 kPa |
373	
374	`[External]` Takaba K, et al. *Orthop J Sports Med* 2022;10(8):23259671221114930. PMID 36003968.
375	
376	The cocked throwing position roughly **doubles** anterior scalene stiffness. This
377	is the cleanest mechanistic link between the throwing motion itself and loading
378	of the interscalene triangle. It measures muscle stiffness, not nerve
379	compression — but it locates the exposure in the throw.
380	
381	**Corroborating anatomy from the largest athlete series:** mean interscalene
382	distance in TOS patients **5.6 ± 3.6 mm**, against cadaveric norms of 10.7–15 mm;
383	and **"hypertrophy of the serratus anterior and posterior scalene muscles was
384	commonly observed in overhead athletes."** `[External]` Funakoshi T, et al. *JSES Int* 2024;8(3):620-9. PMID 38707577.
385	
386	*Note which muscles: posterior scalene and serratus anterior. Those are
387	throwing-driven, not bench-press-driven. This finding is the one a critic could
388	reach for, and it should be presented honestly and in context rather than
389	omitted.*
390	
391	### 2.6 Positional compression is normal — which limits what a positive test means
392	
393	**Established.** MR imaging of 35 asymptomatic volunteers and 54 TOS patients in
394	neutral and provoked positions:
395	
396	- **47% of asymptomatic volunteers** showed positional venous compression at the
397	  prescalene level (vs 63% of patients); **54% vs 61%** costoclavicular.
398	- **Arterial compression: 72% of patients, 0% of volunteers.**
399	- **Nerve compression: 7% of patients, 0% of volunteers.**
400	- "Except for venous thrombosis, vasculonervous compressions were demonstrated
401	  only with arm elevation."
402	
403	`[External]` Demondion X, et al. *Radiology* 2003;227(2):461-8. PMID 12637678.
404	
405	Compression is a positional phenomenon — it does not exist at rest. And roughly
406	half of healthy people compress when you put their arm overhead. Only arterial
407	and nerve compression discriminated.
408	
409	A separate MRI study confirms the spaces are real, measurable and
410	position-dependent, with significant positional change in patients and none in
411	controls. `[External]` Demirbag D, et al. *Arch Phys Med Rehabil* 2007;88(7):844-51. PMID 17601463.
412	
413	### 2.7 Posture and scapular position
414	
415	**Established, with an important correction.** "Droopy shoulder syndrome" is
416	frequently described as costoclavicular narrowing. It is not. Swift & Nichols
417	described low-set shoulders and a long neck, with symptoms that **worsened with
418	downward traction and improved when patients elevated their arms** — the opposite
419	of what compression of a narrowed costoclavicular space predicts. This is a
420	**brachial plexus traction** mechanism. `[External]` Swift TR, Nichols FT. *Neurology* 1984;34(2):212-5. PMID 6538012.
421	
422	**Established in healthy non-athletes.** A short pectoralis minor resting length
423	is associated with a scapula that stays **anteriorly tipped** at higher elevation
424	angles and is **more internally rotated** at lower angles (50 asymptomatic
425	volunteers, electromagnetic motion capture). `[External]` Borstad JD, Ludewig PM. *J Orthop Sports Phys Ther* 2005;35(4):227-38. PMID 15901124.
426	
427	Pectoralis minor length can be measured reliably in the field (coracoid to 4th
428	rib/sternocostal junction; intrarater ICC 0.86–0.97, between-day 0.95).
429	`[External]` Borstad JD. *J Orthop Sports Phys Ther* 2008;38(4):169-74. PMID 18434665. / Rosa DP, et al. *Braz J Phys Ther* 2016;20(2):176-83. PMID 26982455.
430	**No validated numeric cut-off for "short" exists — report the measurement, not a threshold.**
431	
432	**Scope caveat:** this work was done in healthy, asymptomatic, non-athlete adults
433	and targeted subacromial impingement, not TOS. Extending it to throwers *and*
434	from impingement to subcoracoid neurovascular compression is a two-step
435	inference. Reasonable, but **plausible-unproven**.
436	
437	Scapular dyskinesis on the throwing side was commonly documented by 3D-CT in the
438	Funakoshi athlete series — descriptive, not causal.
439	
440	### 2.8 The cervical spine contribution — and a finding from our own library
441	
442	**Established in college pitchers.** 49 healthy college baseball pitchers
443	measured in the 2018 preseason and followed through the season. A Cervical
444	Flexion-Rotation Test finding of ≤39° on the dominant side carried **9.4× the
445	risk** of a >7-day time-loss shoulder or elbow injury (RR 9.38, 95% CI
446	1.28–68.49). Cervical flexion ROM ≤64° carried RR 10.56 (95% CI 1.50–74.34) for
447	pain and disability. Pitchers with restricted rotation were injured earlier
448	(83.6 of 112 days played vs 109.4).
449	`[Zotero: F5YKF6B4, p. 1]` Devaney LL, et al. *Orthop J Sports Med* 2020;8(5):2325967120920556. DOI 10.1177/2325967120920556.
450	
451	Proposed mechanism, `[Zotero: F5YKF6B4, p. 6]`: reduced upper cervical rotation
452	requires compensatory mid-cervical motion, and "these combined motions may
453	decrease the space for the nerve roots in the intervertebral foramina" with
454	consequent myotomal changes impairing scapular and glenohumeral control.
455	
456	**Read this carefully.** Devaney is *not* a TOS study — it measured shoulder and
457	elbow injury. But it establishes, in exactly our population, that **neck mobility
458	is a modifiable, screenable risk factor for throwing injury**, with a mechanism
459	adjacent to the TOS story. The wide confidence intervals (n=49, 10 injuries) mean
460	the 9.4× point estimate should not be quoted as precise; the *direction* and the
461	screening implication are the usable findings.
462	
463	**Plausible but unquantified:** no study quantifies cervical foraminal narrowing
464	as a contributor to nTOS specifically in throwers.
465	
466	### 2.9 What the literature does *not* support
467	
468	- **GIRD → TOS: no evidence whatsoever.** Three separate PubMed queries return
469	  **zero** records. Any such link is speculation. Do not assert it.
470	- **Resistance training causes TOS: unsupported.** No controlled or cohort
471	  evidence. What exists is case reports — a weightlifter with Paget-Schroetter
472	  attributed to bench pressing; a rower/weightlifter with well-developed
473	  scalenes; a weightlifter with subclavian occlusion *confounded by anabolic
474	  steroid use*. `[External]` Crossland DT, Overturf MD. *Cureus* 2024;16(6):e62824. PMID 39036114. / Wong DKH, et al. *JBJS Case Connect* 2021;11(2). PMID 33882031. / Meller L, et al. *Cureus* 2023;15(4):e37763. PMID 37213978.
475	- The closest thing to support for a hypertrophy mechanism in a thrower is a
476	  Division I pitcher with "intermittent axillary artery compression with the arm
477	  in abduction resulting from hypertrophy of the pectoralis minor and scalene
478	  muscles" — attributed to **throwing**, not to a documented lifting programme.
479	  `[External]` Ligh CA, Schulman BL, Safran MR. *Clin Orthop Relat Res* 2009;467(10):2744-8. PMID 19588212.
480	- A 2022 systematic review of TOS in sport located 78 articles: **40 case
481	  reports, 10 clinical studies, 28 reviews**, concluding the field "still lacks
482	  rigorous diagnostic criteria and management guidelines for athletes." That
483	  composition *is* the finding. `[External]` Garraud T, et al. *Front Physiol* 2022;13:838014. PMID 35755427.
484	
485	**The defensible statement:** pectoralis minor and scalene hypertrophy have been
486	documented as the compressing structure in individual athlete case reports, in
487	throwing, water polo, rowing and weightlifting. **Whether training-induced
488	hypertrophy raises TOS risk at a population level has never been tested.**
489

491	
492	## Section 3 — Can lack of endurance or muscle capacity cause TOS?
493	
494	**Direct answer: it is a coherent, mechanistically reasonable hypothesis with no
495	direct empirical support. Act on it because it is cheap, safe, and independently
496	justified — not because the evidence establishes it.**
497	
498	### 3.1 The strongest supporting study
499	
500	**Established finding, contested interpretation.** 100 nTOS patients vs 100
501	healthy controls, isokinetic shoulder rotator testing, with an endurance test
502	defined as 30 repetitions at 180°/s:
503	
504	| Measure | Medial rotators | Lateral rotators |
505	|---|---|---|
506	| Peak strength 60°/s | −21% | −29% |
507	| Peak strength 180°/s | −23% | −20% |
508	| **Endurance (30 reps @ 180°/s)** | **−45%** | **−30%** |
509	
510	All p≤.001, all correlated with QuickDASH. **The endurance deficit is roughly
511	twice the strength deficit** — the single most striking number in this review.
512	`[External]` Daley P, et al. *Diagnostics (Basel)* 2021;11(9):1529. PMID 34573871.
513	
514	**Four constraints block a causal reading. State all four or the claim will not
515	survive scrutiny:**
516	
517	1. **Direction of causation is unresolvable by this design.** nTOS *is* brachial
518	   plexus compression. Reduced fatigue resistance is at least as plausibly a
519	   *consequence* — partial denervation, pain inhibition, disuse, kinesiophobia —
520	   as a cause. A cross-sectional symptomatic-vs-control design cannot separate
521	   them. The authors make no causal claim; they frame it as a diagnostic and
522	   follow-up tool.
523	2. **Wrong muscles.** This measured **glenohumeral rotators** — not scapular
524	   stabilisers, not deep neck flexors, not postural muscles.
525	3. **Wrong population.** 71% female, mean age 39.4 ± 9.6, clinic population.
526	   **Every direct capacity study in TOS is a non-athlete, predominantly female,
527	   ~40-year-old clinic cohort.** Transfer to a 20-year-old pitcher is assumption.
528	4. **The companion study argues for consequence.** Grip **−30%**, key pinch
529	   **−19.5%** vs controls — the classic C8–T1 lower-plexus signature. That
530	   pattern points to nerve compression producing weakness, not the reverse.
531	   `[External]` Fouasson-Chailloux A, et al. *Diagnostics (Basel)* 2021;11(5):874. PMID 34068245.
532	
533	### 3.2 The outright evidentiary blanks
534	
535	- **Scapular stabiliser endurance in TOS vs controls: no study exists.**
536	- **Deep neck flexor endurance in TOS: zero studies.** Complete blank.
537	- **EMG evidence of scalene overactivity during breathing in TOS: none.** The
538	  "accessory breathing → interscalene narrowing" chain is untested. The one
539	  respiratory study found TOS patients had *reduced* MIP, MEP and respiratory
540	  muscle endurance — which if anything is the opposite of the hyperactive-
541	  accessory-breather story, and the authors decline a causal direction.
542	  `[External]` Saglam M, et al. *J Manipulative Physiol Ther* 2020;43(6):606-11. PMID 32829949.
543	- **Nobody has ever measured costoclavicular or retropectoralis minor space
544	  before and after a fatigue protocol.** That single experiment would convert
545	  this from plausibility to mechanism. It has not been run.
546	- **No RCT of exercise therapy versus control for nTOS exists.** The only nTOS
547	  RCT compared surgery to continued conservative care in patients already
548	  refractory to conservative therapy — and all 25 conservative-arm patients
549	  applied for surgery at 3 months. `[External]` Goeteyn J, et al. *Eur J Vasc Endovasc Surg* 2022;64(1):119-27. PMID 35537641.
550	
551	### 3.3 The indirect chain — fatigue alters scapular position
552	
553	**Established (in healthy subjects, acute lab fatigue, framed around subacromial
554	impingement — not the thoracic outlet):**
555	
556	| Study | n | Fatigue protocol | Scapular result |
557	|---|---|---|---|
558	| Tsai 2003 | 30 healthy | External rotation | ↓ posterior tilt, ↓ external rotation, ↓ upward rotation |
559	| Ebaugh 2006 (JOSPT) | 20 healthy | External rotation | ↓ posterior tilt early; **↑** upward rotation mid-range |
560	| Ebaugh 2006 (JEK) | 20 healthy | Repetitive overhead | **↑** upward and external rotation |
561	| Joshi 2011 | 25 overhead athletes | GH external rotation | ↓ lower trapezius activity, **↑** upward rotation |
562	| Harrison 2021 | 30 | Serratus anterior | ↓ posterior tilt, ↑ internal rotation, no change in upward rotation |
563	
564	`[External]` Tsai NT, McClure PW, Karduna AR. *Arch Phys Med Rehabil* 2003;84(7):1000-5. PMID 12881824. / Ebaugh DD, et al. *J Orthop Sports Phys Ther* 2006;36(8):557-71. PMID 16915977; *J Electromyogr Kinesiol* 2006;16(3):224-35. PMID 16125416. / Joshi M, et al. *J Athl Train* 2011;46(4):349-57. PMID 21944066. / Harrison N, Garrett WZ, Timmons MK. *J Sport Rehabil* 2021;30(8):1151-7. PMID 34294607.
565	
566	**Two honest observations:**
567	
568	- **What replicates is decreased posterior tilt (increased anterior tilt).** Four
569	  of five studies show it. Combined with increased internal rotation, that is the
570	  consistent fatigue signature.
571	- **Upward rotation does not replicate.** One study found it decreased, three
572	  found it *increased*, one found no change. **Do not assert a consistent
573	  upward-rotation deficit.**
574	
575	**The inferred chain — label it as inferred:**
576	
577	> scapular muscle fatigue → increased anterior tilt and internal rotation
578	> *(measured, replicated)* → coracoid moves inferoanteriorly, clavicle approaches
579	> the first rib *(anatomically reasoned)* → narrowing of the costoclavicular and
580	> subcoracoid spaces *(spaces are real and position-dependent, but never measured
581	> under fatigue)* → brachial plexus compression *(never demonstrated)*
582	
583	### 3.4 What the treatment protocols actually target
584	
585	A 2026 scoping review screened 1,381 studies and included 29. Exercise appeared
586	in 17/19 (90%) of programmes:
587	
588	- **Stretching (n=15).** Main targets: **scalenes and pectoralis (n=10)**.
589	- **Strengthening (n=14).** Main targets: **scapula (n=9), trapezius and serratus
590	  anterior (n=5)**.
591	- Posture (n=13), manual therapy (n=10), neural mobility (n=7), activity
592	  modification (n=7).
593	
594	`[External]` O'Sullivan J, et al. *Hand Ther* 2026;17589983251411877. PMID 41657761.
595	
596	**So the premise is confirmed at the level of muscle selection — and fails at the
597	level of muscle quality.** The review's own conclusion: *"The reporting of
598	rehabilitation techniques for NTOS is generally poor, particularly regarding
599	treatment intensity."* **No published nTOS protocol specifies sets, reps, loads
600	or time-under-tension in a way that would let you classify it as endurance
601	training.** Anyone asserting "the protocols target endurance specifically" is
602	reading intent into silence.
603	
604	The canonical masterclass describes the core as *"the graded restoration of
605	scapula control, movement, and positioning at rest and through movement"* — that
606	is **motor-control language, not endurance language**. `[External]` Watson LA, Pizzari T, Balster S. *Man Ther* 2010;15(4):305-14. PMID 20382063.
607	
608	**Conservative success rates span a wide, selection-driven range:**
609	
610	| Study | n | Result |
611	|---|---|---|
612	| Novak 1995 | 42 | 25 improved / 10 same / 7 worse (~60%); only 16/42 back to full work + recreation |
613	| Lindgren 1997 | 119 | 88% satisfied at ~25 mo; 73% returned to work (uncontrolled, subjective endpoint) |
614	| **Balderman 2019** | 150 | **Only 40 (27%) satisfactory with PT alone**; 60% went to surgery |
615	| Fouasson-Chailloux 2025 | 182 | 3-week inpatient rehab: **rotator endurance +35–39%**, QuickDASH 57→30 (uncontrolled) |
616	
617	`[External]` Novak CB, Collins ED, Mackinnon SE. *J Hand Surg Am* 1995;20(4):542-8. PMID 7594276. / Lindgren KA. *Arch Phys Med Rehabil* 1997;78(4):373-8. PMID 9111456. / Balderman J, et al. *J Vasc Surg* 2019;70(3):832-41. PMID 30852035. / Fouasson-Chailloux A, et al. *Ann Vasc Surg* 2025;121:603-12. PMID 40907821.
618	
619	27% and 88% are not in conflict — they are opposite ends of a **selection
620	spectrum**. Neither is the number for an athlete. **No cohort anywhere reports
621	what fraction of throwing athletes with nTOS resolve with rehabilitation alone.**
622	For a strength-and-conditioning audience, that is the most important absence in
623	the entire literature.
624	
625	### 3.5 Does injury-prevention programming work in overhead athletes?
626	
627	**Mixed, and weaker than our field generally believes. Know this before citing it.**
628	
629	- **The risk-factor study:** 206 elite male handball players — obvious scapular
630	  dyskinesis OR 8.41 (95% CI 1.47–48.1), external rotation strength OR 0.71 per
631	  10 Nm (0.44–0.99). `[External]` Clarsen B, et al. *Br J Sports Med* 2014;48(17):1327-33. PMID 24948083.
632	- **The replication failed.** Same research group, 329 players — the paper is
633	  subtitled *"previous findings could not be confirmed."* `[External]` Andersson SH, et al. *Br J Sports Med* 2018;52(18):1191-8. PMID 28784621.
634	- **The flagship RCT** (45 teams, 660 players) reduced *any* shoulder problem —
635	  OR 0.72 (0.52–0.98), p=.038 — but **not substantial** shoulder problems: OR
636	  0.78 (0.53–1.16), **p=.23**. `[External]` Andersson SH, et al. *Br J Sports Med* 2017;51(14):1073-80. PMID 27313171.
637	- **The mechanism failed to move.** An RCT of 8 weeks of external rotation band
638	  strengthening produced a between-group difference of **0.06 N/kg (95% CI −0.01
639	  to 0.14)**. Conclusion: *"The ER strength program improved neither the ER
640	  strength nor the ER:IR ratio."* `[External]` Fredriksen H, Cools A, Myklebust G. *J Orthop Sports Phys Ther* 2021;51(4):174-87. PMID 33789429.
641	- **The pooled result is null.** 3 RCTs, n=747: **OR 0.73 (95% CI 0.45–1.17)**.
642	  `[External]` Yonneau J, et al. *BMJ Open Sport Exerc Med* 2025;11(3):e002416. PMID 41035524.
643	- **Baseball's positive RCT used different content.** 16 teams / 237 youth
644	  players, 12-month follow-up, HR 1.940 (95% CI 1.175–3.205), p=.010 favouring
645	  intervention — but the programme was **5 stretching + 2 dynamic mobility + 2
646	  balance exercises, with no scapular strengthening at all.**
647	  `[External]` Sakata J, et al. *Am J Sports Med* 2019;47(11):2709-16. PMID 31336051.
648	
649	### 3.6 Field tests a strength coach could actually use
650	
651	| Test | Normative data | Reliability | Caveat |
652	|---|---|---|---|
653	| **Deep Neck Flexor Endurance** | Men 38.9 ± 20.1 s; women 29.4 ± 13.7 s | ICC(2,k) 0.66 (0.34–0.86) — **moderate at best** | Age and activity level did not affect performance |
654	| **Scapular Muscle Endurance** | **None published** | ICC 0.67, **MDC 30.1 s** | MDC is large relative to hold times — **not good for tracking an individual** |
655	| **CKCUEST** | Collegiate baseball reference values exist | — | Closed-chain stability, not endurance |
656	| **Upper Quarter Y-Balance** | HS baseball/softball: composite 87.2 ± 8.9 %AL, no throwing/non-throwing asymmetry | — | Mobility/stability, not endurance |
657	
658	`[External]` Domenech MA, et al. *PM R* 2011;3(2):105-10. PMID 21333948. / Edmondston SJ, et al. *J Manipulative Physiol Ther* 2008;31(5):348-54. PMID 18558277. / Roush JR, Kitamura J, Waits MC. *N Am J Sports Phys Ther* 2007;2(3):159-63. PMID 21522211. / Butler RJ, et al. *Int J Sports Phys Ther* 2014;9(4):518-24. PMID 25133080.
659	
660	**The decisive caveat: not one of these has ever been validated against TOS.**
661	None has been administered to a TOS population; none has a cut-point for TOS
662	risk. Use them as general upper-quarter capacity monitoring with defensible
663	normative data. **Presenting any of them as a TOS screen would be unsupported.**
664	
665	### 3.7 Verdict
666	
667	**(a) Direct causal evidence that a muscular endurance deficit contributes to
668	TOS: none.** Not weak — absent. No prospective study has measured capacity at
669	baseline and observed who subsequently developed TOS.
670	
671	**(b) Treatment-implies-mechanism reasoning is the strongest strand, and it is
672	structurally circular.** Treatment content tells you what clinicians believe, not
673	what causes the disease.
674	
675	**(c) Pure plausibility carries the rest, and it is well-built plausibility.**
676	Fatigue demonstrably alters scapular position; the outlet spaces are real and
677	position-dependent; anterior tilt plus internal rotation plausibly narrows those
678	corridors. Every link past the kinematics is inference.
679	
680	**The line to use:** *"Building scapular and postural capacity is a
681	mechanistically coherent, low-cost, low-risk intervention that is independently
682	justified by general shoulder health. The claim that it prevents TOS specifically
683	has no direct empirical support."*
684

687	## Section 4 — "Don't lift the pitchers before they throw": is it supported?
688	
689	**Direct answer: no. There is no research supporting this recommendation, and the
690	adjacent evidence leans against it.**
691	
692	### 4.1 The direct evidence does not exist
693	
694	Three structured PubMed queries returned **no baseball study** examining
695	resistance training performed before throwing and its effect on velocity,
696	accuracy, mechanics, kinematics, kinetics, or injury rates. On TOS specifically:
697	**zero papers connect resistance training timing to thoracic outlet syndrome.**
698	
699	### 4.2 The adjacent evidence leans the other way
700	
701	| Study | Protocol | Result |
702	|---|---|---|
703	| Water polo, n=12 | 3×6 @ 80% 1RM (bench, row, half squat) **15 min before** in-water testing | **No difference** in throwing velocity (14.67 vs 14.91 m/s), accuracy, tethered force, swim, or jump (all p>0.05) |
704	| Tennis | 3×6 @ 75% 1RM, maximal intended velocity, not to failure | **No change** in serve/forehand/backhand velocity or accuracy at **3 min, 24 h, or 48 h** |
705	| Trained throwers, n=14 | Morning total-body resistance session | Afternoon overhead throw distance **improved** (p<0.05), 4–6 h later |
706	
707	`[External]` Malliaros I, et al. *Sports (Basel)* 2025;13(11):378. PMID 41295761 — authors state such training "can be safely implemented 15 min prior to in-water training sessions."
708	`[External]` Terraza-Rebollo M, Baiget E. *PLoS One* 2021;16(12):e0260825. PMID 34882729.
709	`[External]` Ekstrand LG, et al. *J Strength Cond Res* 2013;27(1):101-6. PMID 22395279.
710	
711	### 4.3 The one study showing a decrement — and why it undercuts the rule
712	
713	16 adolescent baseball pitchers: push-ups **to failure** and repeated CMJs **to
714	failure** each dropped pitch velocity ~2 km/h (p=0.005).
715	`[External]` Tremblay M, et al. *J Strength Cond Res* 2024;38(8):1447-52. PMID 38838214.
716	
717	1. It used **fatigue to failure**, not a programmed lift.
718	2. The **recovery interval before re-test was not quantified**. Pilot,
719	   non-randomised.
720	3. **Lower-body fatigue dropped velocity as much as upper-body fatigue.** If the
721	   mechanism were loading the throwing arm, squatting should not have mattered
722	   equally. This contradicts the rationale the rule rests on.
723	
724	### 4.4 The mechanistic chain breaks at the end
725	
726	- **Fatigue degrades shoulder proprioception** — robust and replicated.
727	  `[External]` Carpenter JE, Blasier RB, Pellizzon GG. *Am J Sports Med* 1998;26(2):262-5. PMID 9548121. / Tripp BL, et al. *J Athl Train* 2004;39(4):316-20. PMID 15592603.
728	- **But the deficit does not become functional.** A **160% increase in joint
729	  repositioning error** produced **no change** in motor control (Y-Balance Upper
730	  Quarter) or performance (Athletic Shoulder test). `[External]` Hadjisavvas S, et al. *Hum Mov Sci* 2024;98:103299. PMID 39461122.
731	- **Recovery is fast.** After throwing-to-fatigue in 16 collegiate players,
732	  scapulothoracic, glenohumeral, elbow and endpoint acuity **recovered within 4–7
733	  minutes**. The one exception: **glenohumeral acuity in the arm-cocked position
734	  had not recovered at 10 minutes.** `[External]` Tripp BL, Yochem EM, Uhl TL. *J Athl Train* 2007;42(4):452-7. PMID 18174932.
735	- **Counterweight:** strength training is associated with *better* shoulder
736	  proprioception chronically. `[External]` Salles JI, et al. *J Athl Train* 2015;50(3):277-80. PMID 25594912.
737	- All the fatigue-alters-pitching-mechanics literature concerns fatigue **from
738	  throwing itself**. `[External]` Murray TA, et al. *Am J Sports Med* 2001;29(2):137-42. PMID 11292037. / Birfer R, Sonne MW, Holmes MW. *PeerJ* 2019;7:e7390. PMID 31392098.
739	
740	That arm-cocked exception is the **single most defensible mechanistic hook** for
741	the athletic training staff's concern. It is narrow, and it is about the cocked
742	position specifically.
743	
744	### 4.5 The defensible version
745	
746	| Rationale | Support |
747	|---|---|
748	| (a) Manage **total daily/weekly load** | **Best supported**, but indirectly — the literature is about cumulative *throwing* load |
749	| (b) Avoid **heavy loading of the throwing shoulder** specifically | **Not supported, actively undercut** |
750	| (c) **Proximity in hours** | **Weak** — 15 min fine, 3 min fine, 4–6 h beneficial |
751	| (d) Nothing at all | **Closest to the truth for the blanket rule** |
752	
753	**Recommended reframe:** *avoid taking the upper body to failure, and avoid novel
754	heavy eccentric upper-body work, in the hours before a high-intent throwing
755	session.* A dose-and-proximity-to-failure statement. Every trial using a dosed,
756	sub-failure lift found no impairment.
757	
758	Present the current rule as **conservative professional judgment — a legitimate
759	basis for a decision — but not as research-backed.** There is no NSCA or ACSM
760	baseball-specific position statement, and no MLB/ASMI consensus, prescribing
761	lifting-relative-to-throwing order.
762	
763	---
764	
765	## Section 5 — Softball-specific evidence and workload
766	
767	### 5.1 The softball TOS literature barely exists
768	
769	PubMed `"thoracic outlet"[TIAB] AND softball[TIAB]` returns **exactly 6 records**:
770	
771	- **2 case reports in softball athletes**, both **structural/congenital first-rib
772	  pathology** — a fracture nonunion and a congenital pseudarthrosis. **Neither
773	  identifies the patient as a pitcher.** `[External]` Young BL, et al. *J Shoulder Elbow Surg* 2016;25(11):e353-7. PMID 27742249. / Gibson TW, Carson L. *JBJS Case Connect* 2021;11(3). PMID 34329202.
774	- **4 cohort studies where softball is pooled with baseball** or given only as a
775	  prevalence.
776	
777	A systematic review of Paget-Schroetter syndrome in athletes **does not contain
778	the word "softball"** — zero softball effort-thrombosis cases in the systematic
779	literature. `[External]` Keller RE, et al. *J Shoulder Elbow Surg* 2020;29(11):2417-25. PMID 32868012.
780	
781	**Net: no peer-reviewed paper attributes TOS or effort thrombosis in a softball
782	pitcher to the pitching motion.** The design ceiling across the entire softball
783	TOS literature is the single case report. Every mechanistic claim must be
784	extrapolated from baseball, and the extrapolation should be stated.
785	
786	### 5.2 The windmill is not load-sparing
787	
788	| Measure | Value | Source |
789	|---|---|---|
790	| Shoulder distraction, youth | **94% body weight** | Werner 2005, n=53 |
791	| Shoulder distraction, elite/Olympic | **80% BW** | Werner 2006, n=24 |
792	| Peak compression, shoulder & elbow | **70–98% BW** | Barrentine 1998, n=8 |
793	| Shoulder extension/abduction torque | **9–10% BW × height** | Barrentine 1998 |
794	| **Peak biceps activation, windmill vs overhand (velocity-matched)** | **38% vs 19%** | Rojas 2009 |
795	| Scapular excursion through the pitch | 5–22° per plane | Holtz 2026, n=17 |
796	
797	`[External]` Werner SL, et al. *Am J Sports Med* 2005;33(4):552-60. PMID 15722291; 2006;34(4):597-603. PMID 16282576. / Barrentine SW, et al. *J Orthop Sports Phys Ther* 1998;28(6):405-15. PMID 9836172. / Rojas IL, et al. *Am J Sports Med* 2009;37(3):558-65. PMID 19174551. / Holtz KA, et al. *Int J Sports Med* 2026;47(1):72-7. PMID 40738124.
798	
799	Three independent sources state windmill shoulder and elbow loads are **similar
800	to baseball pitching**. Our own library says the same:
801	`[Zotero: FGQAC8DL, p. 1]` — *"it is continually reported that the shoulder stress
802	endured from the softball pitch is analogous to that of the baseball pitch,"* and
803	shoulder injury rates and patterns are "comparable with those reported in the
804	sport of baseball." Oliver GD, et al. *Orthop J Sports Med* 2019;7(8):2325967119865171.
805	
806	**The "windmill is a natural motion" belief is explicitly named as a
807	misconception in the peer-reviewed literature.** At matched ball velocity, biceps
808	demand is **double** the overhand throw.
809	
810	**Hyperabduction — label as inference.** The windmill carries the arm through
811	full overhead elevation once per pitch, transiently and at high angular velocity.
812	**No windmill study reports maximum shoulder elevation angle or time above 90°.**
813	The plausible outlet link is cumulative repetition, not sustained positional
814	narrowing.
815	
816	**The actionable lever is proximal.** Lower-extremity screening alone predicted
817	**49.9%** of peak shoulder distraction variance in 46 collegiate pitchers, rising
818	to **56.2%** with hip rotation strength. `[External]` Ulman SM, et al. *Am J Sports Med* 2025;53(3):565-70. PMID 39844736.
819	
820	Our library adds the trunk side: at foot contact, increased trunk rotation toward
821	the pitching arm, increased stride length and a posteriorly shifted COM explained
822	**~33% of variance** in upper-extremity pain among 37 D1 softball pitchers.
823	`[Zotero: FGQAC8DL, p. 1 and p. 4]`
824	
825	### 5.3 Workload — the strongest part of the case
826	
827	**Rules, verified: NCAA softball has NO pitch count limit and NO mandated rest.**
828	Confirmed three ways (Zaremski 2025 states "no established pitch count guidelines
829	for collegiate softball"; Freetly et al. Table 2 lists NCAA for both sports as
830	"No restrictions / None"; the NCAA softball playing-rules page lists no such
831	document). NCAA baseball likewise has none — but **NFHS Rule 6-2-6 requires every
832	state association to adopt a baseball pitch-count restriction with mandated
833	rest**, while NFHS softball is capped only by *innings*.
