1. J Plast Reconstr Aesthet Surg. 2025 Dec;111:86-92. doi: 
10.1016/j.bjps.2025.09.034. Epub 2025 Oct 4.

Timing matters: Early versus delayed surgery for neurogenic thoracic outlet 
syndrome and its impact on reoperation and pain outcomes.

Phuyal D(1), Ting J(1), Hoffner N(1), Yacoub S(1), Darras O(1), Chim H(2).

(1)Cleveland Clinic Foundation, Cleveland, OH, USA.
(2)Division of Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, Department of Surgery, 
Louisiana State University Health Sciences Center, New Orleans, LA, USA. 
Electronic address: harveychim@yahoo.com.

INTRODUCTION: We evaluated the impact of the timing of brachial plexus 
neurolysis in conjunction with rib sparing scalenectomy or first rib resection 
on surgical and pain-related outcomes by comparing patients who underwent 
surgery within 3 months of diagnosis of neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome 
(early) to those operated after 3 months (delayed).
METHODS: This is a propensity-matched, multi-institutional retrospective 
database study. Patient demographics and surgical and pain outcomes were 
collected for 5 years after surgery. We used the Chi-squared test and logistic 
regression for analysis.
RESULTS: A total of 2593 patients were included (n=1380 early; n=1213 delayed). 
After 1:1 propensity matching (n=1069), there was no difference in pneumothorax, 
hemorrhage, infection, or re-do neurolysis procedure between the groups. Acute 
pain did not significantly differ between the groups. Chronic pain outcomes 
favored early surgery. At 6 months, the chronic pain rate was significantly 
lower in the early group (6.83% vs. 10.3%; OR 0.66 [0.50-0.88]; p<0.005), and 
this trend persisted through 5 years (14.5% vs. 22.36%; OR 0.65 [0.54-0.78]; 
p<0.0001). The rate of myalgia was also lower in the early cohort at 3 months 
(1.03% vs. 2.81%; OR 0.37 [0.19-0.73]; p<0.005), and this trend persisted 
through 5 years (6.83% vs. 11.79%; OR 0.58 [0.44-0.76]; p<0.0001).
CONCLUSION: Early surgery within 3 months of presentation for patients with 
neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome is associated with significantly reduced 
long-term rates of chronic pain and myalgia. These findings support early 
surgical intervention to optimize pain-related outcomes. Our results should be 
interpreted by considering the variable symptom duration prior to diagnosis, as 
this may affect the observed benefit of early surgery.

Surgeons. Published by Elsevier Ltd. All rights reserved.




2. ISRN Neurol. 2013 Sep 10;2013:673020. doi: 10.1155/2013/673020. eCollection 
2013.

Early versus Late Surgical Treatment for Neurogenic Thoracic Outlet Syndrome.

Al-Hashel JY(1), El Shorbgy AA, Ahmed SF, Elshereef RR.

(1)Department of Neurology, Ibn Sina Hospital, P.O. Box 25427, Safat 13115, 
Kuwait ; Department of Medicine, Kuwait University, P.O. Box 24923, Safat 13110, 
Kuwait.

Objectives. To compare the outcome of early surgical intervention versus late 
surgical treatment in cases of neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome (NTOS). 
Design. Prospective study. Settings. Secondary care (Al-Minia University 
Hospital, Egypt) from 2007 to 2010. Participants. Thirty-five patients of NTOS 
(25 women and 10 men, aged 20-52 years), were classified into 2 groups. First 
group (20 patients) was operated within 3 months of the onset and the second 
group (15 patients) was operated 6 months after physiotherapy. Interventions. 
All patients were operated via supraclavicular surgical approach. Outcomes 
Measures. Both groups were evaluated clinically and, neurophysiologically and 
answered the disabilities of the arm, shoulder, and hand (DASH) questionnaire 
preoperatively and 6 months after the surgery. Results. Paraesthesia, pain, and 
sensory nerve action potential (SNAP) of ulnar nerve were significantly improved 
in group one. Muscle weakness and denervation in electromyography EMG were less 
frequent in group one. The postoperative DASH score improved in both groups but 
it was less significant in group two (P < .001 in group 1 and P < .05 in group 
2). Conclusions. Surgical treatment of NTOS improves functional disability and 
stop degeneration of the nerves. Early surgical treatment decreases the 
occurrence of muscle wasting and denervation of nerves compared to late surgery.

PMCID: PMC3784157


3. Eur J Cardiothorac Surg. 2004 Feb;25(2):173-8. doi:
10.1016/j.ejcts.2003.11.021.

Clinical predictors of surgical outcome in patients with thoracic outlet 
syndrome operated on via transaxillary approach.

Yavuzer S(1), Atinkaya C, Tokat O.

(1)Department of Thoracic Surgery, Ankara University Faculty of Medicine, Ibn-i 
Sina Hospital, 06100, Sihhiye, Ankara, Turkey. yavuzers@hotmail.com

OBJECTIVES: Although the transaxillary route appears to be the optimal approach 
in patients with thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS), the effect of clinical features 
on surgical outcome remains unclear. We conducted a study to determine the 
clinical predictors of surgical outcome in patients with TOS.
METHODS: We examined the data charts of patients with TOS who underwent 
operation via transaxillary approach. We investigated the possible correlations 
between the clinical features and surgical outcomes, and analyzed the data with 
logistic regression model to clarify the effect of clinical features on surgical 
outcome.
RESULTS: A total of 127 patients with a mean age of 32.1+/-10.0 years (range 
14-62 years) were analyzed. The rates of favorable and poor surgical outcomes 
were 82.7 and 17.3%, respectively. The subgroups of symptom duration (P=0.023), 
the subgroups of ulnar nerve conduction velocity (P=0.033) and the presence of 
cervical rib (P=0.003) showed a significant correlation with surgical outcome. 
Multivariate analysis revealed that the shorter duration of symptoms (P=0.017) 
and the presence of a cervical rib (P=0.026) had a significantly unfavorable 
effect on surgical outcome.
CONCLUSIONS: The shorter duration of symptoms and the presence of a cervical rib 
may imply an unfavorable surgical outcome in patients with TOS.



4. J Vasc Surg. 2017 Dec;66(6):1798-1805. doi: 10.1016/j.jvs.2017.06.108. Epub
2017  Sep 21.

Midterm and long-term follow-up in competitive athletes undergoing thoracic 
outlet decompression for neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome.

Shutze W(1), Richardson B(2), Shutze R(3), Tran K(3), Dao A(3), Ogola GO(4), 
Young A(5), Pearl G(6).

(1)The Heart Hospital Baylor Plano, Plano, Tex. Electronic address: 
willshut@sbcglobal.net.
(2)Department of General Surgery, Baylor University Medical Center, Dallas, Tex.
(3)Texas Vascular Associates, Plano, Tex.
(4)Office of the Chief Quality Officer, Baylor Scott and White Health, Dallas, 
Tex.
(5)Division of Vascular Surgery, Baylor University Medical Center, Dallas, Tex.
(6)Division of Vascular Surgery, Baylor Heart and Vascular Hospital, Dallas, 
Tex.

BACKGROUND: Neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome (NTOS) results from compression 
of the brachial plexus by the clavicle, first rib, and scalene muscles and may 
develop secondary to repetitive motion of the upper extremity. Athletes 
routinely perform repetitive motions, and sports requiring significant arm and 
shoulder use may put the participant at increased risk for NTOS. Competitive 
athletes who develop NTOS may require first rib resection and scalenectomy 
(FRRS) for symptomatic relief. However, the effectiveness of FRRS has not 
previously been studied in this vulnerable population.
METHODS: This is a cross-sectional study of competitive athletes with NTOS who 
received FRRS by the senior author between 2009 and 2014. Eligible patients were 
contacted by phone and invited to complete a nine-item survey assessing the 
long-term effects of FRRS on pain medication use, postoperative physical therapy 
duration, patient satisfaction, symptom relief, activities of daily living, 
athletic performance, time to return of athletic performance, and need for other 
operations. Multivariate analyses of the following risk factors were performed: 
age, pectoralis minor release, preoperative narcotic use, athletic shutdown, and 
involvement in a throwing sport.
RESULTS: There were 232 competitive athletes who met the inclusion criteria, and 
67 of these (age, 14-48 years; 35 male; 99% white) responded to the survey. The 
average time between surgery and survey completion was 3.9 years (range, 
2.2-7.0 years). The most frequent sports conducted by this group were baseball 
and softball (n = 44 [66%]), volleyball (n = 7 [10%]), and cheerleading and 
gymnastics (n = 5 [7%]), ranging from high-school to professional levels. The 
survey results revealed that 96% were improved in pain medication use, 75% would 
undergo FRRS on the contralateral side if needed, 82% had resolution of 
symptoms, and 94% were able to perform activities of daily living without 
limitation; 70% returned to the same or better level of athletic activity after 
FRRS, and this occurred within 1 year in 50%. Multivariate regression analysis 
identified younger age as a predictor of the length of physical therapy and 
preoperative narcotics use as a predictor of symptom resolution.
CONCLUSIONS: At our center, >40% of patients requiring FRRS for NTOS are 
competitive athletes. The results of this study show that the majority of them 
are able to return to their precompetitive state after FRRS, and few experience 
limitations in their daily living activities. Half can return to competition at 
or exceeding their premorbid ability level within 6 months of surgery. The 
majority are pleased with their decision to undergo FRRS. Further investigation 
is needed to identify predictive factors for successful return to competitive 
athletics.

rights reserved.



5. J Vasc Surg. 2014 Oct;60(4):1012-7; discussion 1017-8. doi: 
10.1016/j.jvs.2014.04.013. Epub 2014 May 14.

Thoracic outlet syndrome in high-performance athletes.

Chandra V(1), Little C(1), Lee JT(2).

(1)Division of Vascular Surgery, Stanford University Medical Center, Stanford, 
Calif.
(2)Division of Vascular Surgery, Stanford University Medical Center, Stanford, 
Calif. Electronic address: jtlee@stanford.edu.

OBJECTIVE: Repetitive upper extremity use in high-performance athletes is 
associated with the development of neurogenic and vascular thoracic outlet 
syndrome (TOS). Surgical therapy in appropriately selected patients can provide 
relief of symptoms and protection from future disability. We sought to determine 
the incidence and timing of competitive athletes to return to their prior 
high-performance level after TOS treatment and surgery.
METHODS: We reviewed all competitive high school, collegiate, and professional 
athletes treated for venous or neurogenic TOS (nTOS) from 2000 to 2012. Patient 
demographics, workup, and treatment approaches were recorded and analyzed. 
Patients with nTOS were assessed with quality of life surveys using the 
previously validated 11-item version of the Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder 
and Hand (QuickDASH) scale, scored from 0 to 100 (100 = worse). Return to full 
athletic activity was defined as returning to prior competitive high school, 
collegiate, or professional sports.
RESULTS: During the study period, 41 competitive athletes (44% female) with a 
mean age of 19 years, were treated, comprising 13 baseball/softball players, 11 
swimmers, 5 water polo players, 4 rowers, 2 volleyball players, 2 synchronized 
swimmers, 1 wrestler, 1 diver, 1 weightlifter, and 1 football player. 
Twenty-seven athletes (66%) were treated for nTOS, and 14 (34%) had 
Paget-Schroetter syndrome (PSS). All PSS patients underwent typical treatment of 
consisting of thrombolysis/anticoagulation, followed by first rib resection. 
Most nTOS patients were treated according to our previously reported highly 
selective algorithm, beginning with TOS-specific physical therapy (PT) after the 
clinical diagnosis was made. Because of mild to modest symptom improvement after 
PT, 67% of the nTOS athletes evaluated ultimately underwent supraclavicular 
first rib resection and brachial plexus neurolysis. Return to full competitive 
athletics was achieved in 85% of all patients, including 93% of the PSS patients 
and 81% of the nTOS athletes, at an average of 4.6 months after the 
intervention. In the nTOS cohort successfully returning to prior sports ability, 
seven (32%) were treated only with PT. Of those athletes who underwent surgery 
for nTOS, 83% returned to full competitive levels. QuickDASH disability scores 
improved from a mean of 40.4 preoperatively to 11.7 postoperatively, indicating 
significant improvement in symptoms after treatment. Recurrence of symptoms was 
noted in two nTOS (7%) and two PSS (14%) athletes.
CONCLUSIONS: Standardized treatment algorithms for venous and nTOS and 
aggressive TOS-specific PT are key components to optimizing clinical outcomes in 
this special cohort of TOS patients. Most athletes treated for venous and nTOS 
can successfully return to competitive sports at their prior high-performance 
level.

rights reserved.



6. J Vasc Surg. 2012 Oct;56(4):1061-7; discussion 1068. doi: 
10.1016/j.jvs.2012.03.262. Epub 2012 Jul 6.

Management of unresolved, recurrent, and/or contralateral neurogenic symptoms in 
patients following first rib resection and scalenectomy.

Rochlin DH(1), Likes KC, Gilson MM, Christo PJ, Freischlag JA.

(1)Division of Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy, Johns Hopkins Medical 
Institutions, Baltimore, MD, USA. danielle.rochlin@jhmi.edu

BACKGROUND: Surgical treatment for neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome does not 
always yield successful outcomes. The purpose of this study was to describe 
patients with unresolved, recurrent, and/or contralateral symptoms following 
first rib resection and scalenectomy (FRRS) and to determine therapies for 
improving their outcomes.
METHODS: Data on 161 neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome patients (182 FRRS 
procedures) were prospectively collected from 2003 to 2011 and retrospectively 
reviewed for evidence of unresolved, recurrent, and/or contralateral neurogenic 
symptoms following FRRS. Demographic and clinical characteristics, 
interventions, and outcomes were compared between these patients and those with 
a successful result.
RESULTS: Twenty-three patients (24 FRRS) had unresolved symptoms at a mean of 
16.1 ± 14.7 postoperative months. Compared with successes, these patients were 
older (mean age, 45 vs 38 years; P = .002) and active smokers (33% vs 13%; P = 
.031), with a longer duration of symptoms (90 vs 48 months; P = .005). They had 
higher rates of chronic pain syndromes (67% vs 14%; P < .001), neck and/or 
shoulder comorbidities (58% vs 22%; P < .001), preoperative opioid use (67% vs 
31%; P = .001), and preoperative Botox injections (46% vs 20%; P = .009) with 
less relief (18% vs 64%; P = .014). Sixteen patients had recurrent symptoms at a 
mean of 12.1 ± 9.7 postoperative months. These patients had more chronic pain 
syndromes (38%; P = .028) and neck and/or shoulder comorbidities (50%; P = 
.027), with recurrence secondary to scar tissue (69%; P < .001) and reinjury 
(31%; P = .002). Postoperative treatments for both groups included physical 
therapy and local injections, where six unresolved (26%) and 13 recurrent (81%) 
patients achieved freedom from opioids at the end of the follow-up period. 
Twenty-one patients had contralateral symptoms and underwent secondary FRRS at a 
mean of 15.0 months (range, 7-30 months) following primary FRRS. The first 
operation was successful in 90% of cases.
CONCLUSIONS: Patients with unresolved symptoms are older, active smokers with 
more comorbid pain syndromes, neck and/or shoulder disease, and a longer symptom 
duration. These patients face a more difficult recovery, whereas patients with 
recurrent symptoms are well managed with physical therapy and Botox injections. 
Patients with contralateral symptoms at >1 year are effectively treated with 
secondary FRRS. Patients must be followed closely after FRRS to determine if 
additional interventions are necessary to ensure successful results.

rights reserved.



7. Chir Main. 2012 Oct;31(5):244-9. doi: 10.1016/j.main.2012.08.005. Epub 2012
Sep  26.

[True neurological thoracic outlet syndrome. Retrospective study of 30 
consecutive cases].

[Article in French]

Marty FL(1), Corcia P, Alexandre J, Laulan J.

(1)Services de chirurgie orthopédique et traumatologique 1 et 2, unité de 
chirurgie de la main, hôpital Trousseau, CHU de Tours, 37044 Tours cedex, 
France.

OBJECTIVES: Neurologic TOS with amyotrophy is exceptional and the diagnosis is 
usually delayed compromising the outcome after treatment. The aims of this study 
were to define clinical features, anatomical causes, surgical results and 
prognostic factors of this disease.
METHODS: All of the TOS with objective neurologic deficit treated in our unit 
between 1989 and 2011 were assessed retrospectively. Thirty cases were 
identified in 28 patients (two bilateral cases). The mean-age was 44 years (16 
to 70).
RESULTS: Muscular atrophy always predominated in the lateral thenar muscles. 
Seventeen also had sensory symptoms. Twenty-two patients (24 cases) were 
surgically treated. Twenty-three cases could be assessed with a mean follow-up 
of 39 months. Recovery was complete in four cases (17%), marked in nine cases 
(39%) and minimal in ten cases (44%).
CONCLUSIONS: Neurological TOS with objective manifestations have to be 
distinguished from other types of neurological TOS. Muscular atrophy in the hand 
appears insidiously and the pain, which is inconstant, stays always in the 
background. Duration of symptoms before surgical treatment is the main 
prognostic factor.




8. J Vasc Surg. 2026 Jul 8:S0741-5214(26)01430-8. doi: 10.1016/j.jvs.2026.06.158.
 Online ahead of print.

Patient reported long-term quality of life and symptom resolution after first 
rib resection and anterior scalenectomy.

Linden J(1), Faber L(2), Sutton L(3), Villenthi A(4), Goldman M(3), Chang K(3), 
Velazquez G(3), Freischlag JA(3), Stutsrim A(3).

(1)Wake Forest University School of Medicine, Winston-Salem, NC. Electronic 
address: justin.linden@wfusm.edu.
(2)Wake Forest University School of Medicine, Winston-Salem, NC.
(3)Department of Endovascular and Vascular Surgery, Atrium Health Wake Forest 
Baptist Medical Center, Winston-Salem, NC.
(4)Department of Biostatistics and Data Science, Wake Forest University School 
of Medicine, Winston-Salem, NC.

OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study was to evaluate patient-reported long-term 
outcomes in patients with neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome (nTOS) and venous 
TOS (vTOS), who underwent first rib resection and anterior scalenectomy (FRRAS).
METHODS: Single institution, retrospective chart review from 2015 to 2025 was 
completed after obtaining institutional review board approval. Baseline 
demographic and clinical data were collected for patients who underwent surgery 
at least 1 year earlier. A five-question quality of life (QOL) survey was 
provided to patients through phone call or the electronic health record. 
Descriptive statistics including number (%) of categorical factors or median and 
interquartile range of continuous factors were reported. Differences between TOS 
subtypes were assessed using Fisher exact test (categorical) or rank-sum tests 
(continuous).
RESULTS: Of the 204 patients who underwent FRRAS, 104 completed our survey 
(57/114 nTOS and 47/90 vTOS). Patients with nTOS had significantly longer 
preoperative symptom duration (median [interquartile range], 24 [12-60] vs 2 
[1-10] months for vTOS; P < .001) with no other differences between groups. In 
nTOS, most patients (43/57, 75.4%) indicated improved QOL, regardless of the 
surgical approach. Although most patients did not have recurrent symptoms 
(32/57, 56.1%), those who did were more likely to be older (median age, 39 
[35-46] vs 27 [17-39] years; P = .003). 30/57 patients (52.6%) reported ongoing 
paresthesias, though 47/57 patients (82.5%) did not require chronic medications. 
Patients requiring chronic medication were more likely to have undergone 
reoperative surgery (30% vs 4.3%; P = .033). Similarly, in vTOS, most patients 
(41/47, 87.2%) reported improved QOL, regardless of the surgical approach. Most 
veins (45/47, 95.7%) were patent at the time of follow-up and did not affect 
outcome. Younger patients were more likely to have improvement (median, 31 
[22-41] vs 47 [44-50] years; P = .015). Patients with recurrent symptoms, 
paresthesias, chronic medication use, or ongoing physical therapy/occupational 
therapy needs were significantly older (median age: 49 [43-53] vs 30 [21-39] 
years, P < .001; 42 [31-48] vs 30 [20-41] years, P = .027; 52 [50-55] vs 32

INTRODUCTION: We evaluated the impact of the timing of brachial plexus 
neurolysis in conjunction with rib sparing scalenectomy or first rib resection 
on surgical and pain-related outcomes by comparing patients who underwent 
surgery within 3 months of diagnosis of neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome 
(early) to those operated after 3 months (delayed).
METHODS: This is a propensity-matched, multi-institutional retrospective 
database study. Patient demographics and surgical and pain outcomes were 
collected for 5 years after surgery. We used the Chi-squared test and logistic 
regression for analysis.
RESULTS: A total of 2593 patients were included (n=1380 early; n=1213 delayed). 
After 1:1 propensity matching (n=1069), there was no difference in pneumothorax, 
hemorrhage, infection, or re-do neurolysis procedure between the groups. Acute 
pain did not significantly differ between the groups. Chronic pain outcomes 
favored early surgery. At 6 months, the chronic pain rate was significantly 
lower in the early group (6.83% vs. 10.3%; OR 0.66 [0.50-0.88]; p<0.005), and 
this trend persisted through 5 years (14.5% vs. 22.36%; OR 0.65 [0.54-0.78]; 
p<0.0001). The rate of myalgia was also lower in the early cohort at 3 months 
(1.03% vs. 2.81%; OR 0.37 [0.19-0.73]; p<0.005), and this trend persisted 
through 5 years (6.83% vs. 11.79%; OR 0.58 [0.44-0.76]; p<0.0001).
CONCLUSION: Early surgery within 3 months of presentation for patients with 
neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome is associated with significantly reduced 
long-term rates of chronic pain and myalgia. These findings support early 
surgical intervention to optimize pain-related outcomes. Our results should be 
interpreted by considering the variable symptom duration prior to diagnosis, as 
this may affect the observed benefit of early surgery.

BACKGROUND: Neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome (NTOS) results from compression 
of the brachial plexus by the clavicle, first rib, and scalene muscles and may 
develop secondary to repetitive motion of the upper extremity. Athletes 
routinely perform repetitive motions, and sports requiring significant arm and 
shoulder use may put the participant at increased risk for NTOS. Competitive 
athletes who develop NTOS may require first rib resection and scalenectomy 
(FRRS) for symptomatic relief. However, the effectiveness of FRRS has not 
previously been studied in this vulnerable population.
METHODS: This is a cross-sectional study of competitive athletes with NTOS who 
received FRRS by the senior author between 2009 and 2014. Eligible patients were 
contacted by phone and invited to complete a nine-item survey assessing the 
long-term effects of FRRS on pain medication use, postoperative physical therapy 
duration, patient satisfaction, symptom relief, activities of daily living, 
athletic performance, time to return of athletic performance, and need for other 
operations. Multivariate analyses of the following risk factors were performed: 
age, pectoralis minor release, preoperative narcotic use, athletic shutdown, and 
involvement in a throwing sport.

67 of these (age, 14-48 years; 35 male; 99% white) responded to the survey. The 
average time between surgery and survey completion was 3.9 years (range, 
2.2-7.0 years). The most frequent sports conducted by this group were baseball 
and softball (n = 44 [66%]), volleyball (n = 7 [10%]), and cheerleading and 
gymnastics (n = 5 [7%]), ranging from high-school to professional levels. The 
survey results revealed that 96% were improved in pain medication use, 75% would 
undergo FRRS on the contralateral side if needed, 82% had resolution of 
symptoms, and 94% were able to perform activities of daily living without 
limitation; 70% returned to the same or better level of athletic activity after 
FRRS, and this occurred within 1 year in 50%. Multivariate regression analysis 
identified younger age as a predictor of the length of physical therapy and 
preoperative narcotics use as a predictor of symptom resolution.

competitive athletes. The results of this study show that the majority of them 
are able to return to their precompetitive state after FRRS, and few experience 
limitations in their daily living activities. Half can return to competition at 
or exceeding their premorbid ability level within 6 months of surgery. The 
majority are pleased with their decision to undergo FRRS. Further investigation 
is needed to identify predictive factors for successful return to competitive 
athletics.

associated with the development of neurogenic and vascular thoracic outlet 
syndrome (TOS). Surgical therapy in appropriately selected patients can provide 
relief of symptoms and protection from future disability. We sought to determine 
the incidence and timing of competitive athletes to return to their prior 
high-performance level after TOS treatment and surgery.

athletes treated for venous or neurogenic TOS (nTOS) from 2000 to 2012. Patient 
demographics, workup, and treatment approaches were recorded and analyzed.

previously validated 11-item version of the Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder 
and Hand (QuickDASH) scale, scored from 0 to 100 (100 = worse). Return to full 
athletic activity was defined as returning to prior competitive high school, 
collegiate, or professional sports.

mean age of 19 years, were treated, comprising 13 baseball/softball players, 11 
swimmers, 5 water polo players, 4 rowers, 2 volleyball players, 2 synchronized 
swimmers, 1 wrestler, 1 diver, 1 weightlifter, and 1 football player.

Paget-Schroetter syndrome (PSS). All PSS patients underwent typical treatment of 
consisting of thrombolysis/anticoagulation, followed by first rib resection.

selective algorithm, beginning with TOS-specific physical therapy (PT) after the 
clinical diagnosis was made. Because of mild to modest symptom improvement after 
PT, 67% of the nTOS athletes evaluated ultimately underwent supraclavicular 
first rib resection and brachial plexus neurolysis. Return to full competitive 
athletics was achieved in 85% of all patients, including 93% of the PSS patients

BACKGROUND: Surgical treatment for neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome does not 
always yield successful outcomes. The purpose of this study was to describe 
patients with unresolved, recurrent, and/or contralateral symptoms following 
first rib resection and scalenectomy (FRRS) and to determine therapies for 
improving their outcomes.
METHODS: Data on 161 neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome patients (182 FRRS 
procedures) were prospectively collected from 2003 to 2011 and retrospectively 
reviewed for evidence of unresolved, recurrent, and/or contralateral neurogenic 
symptoms following FRRS. Demographic and clinical characteristics, 
interventions, and outcomes were compared between these patients and those with 
a successful result.
RESULTS: Twenty-three patients (24 FRRS) had unresolved symptoms at a mean of 
16.1 ± 14.7 postoperative months. Compared with successes, these patients were 
older (mean age, 45 vs 38 years; P = .002) and active smokers (33% vs 13%; P = 
.031), with a longer duration of symptoms (90 vs 48 months; P = .005). They had 
higher rates of chronic pain syndromes (67% vs 14%; P < .001), neck and/or 
shoulder comorbidities (58% vs 22%; P < .001), preoperative opioid use (67% vs 
31%; P = .001), and preoperative Botox injections (46% vs 20%; P = .009) with 
less relief (18% vs 64%; P = .014). Sixteen patients had recurrent symptoms at a 
mean of 12.1 ± 9.7 postoperative months. These patients had more chronic pain 
syndromes (38%; P = .028) and neck and/or shoulder comorbidities (50%; P = 
.027), with recurrence secondary to scar tissue (69%; P < .001) and reinjury 
(31%; P = .002). Postoperative treatments for both groups included physical 
therapy and local injections, where six unresolved (26%) and 13 recurrent (81%) 
patients achieved freedom from opioids at the end of the follow-up period. 
Twenty-one patients had contralateral symptoms and underwent secondary FRRS at a 
mean of 15.0 months (range, 7-30 months) following primary FRRS. The first 
operation was successful in 90% of cases.
CONCLUSIONS: Patients with unresolved symptoms are older, active smokers with 
more comorbid pain syndromes, neck and/or shoulder disease, and a longer symptom 
duration. These patients face a more difficult recovery, whereas patients with 
recurrent symptoms are well managed with physical therapy and Botox injections. 
Patients with contralateral symptoms at >1 year are effectively treated with 
secondary FRRS. Patients must be followed closely after FRRS to determine if 
additional interventions are necessary to ensure successful results.

OBJECTIVES: Neurologic TOS with amyotrophy is exceptional and the diagnosis is 
usually delayed compromising the outcome after treatment. The aims of this study 
were to define clinical features, anatomical causes, surgical results and 
prognostic factors of this disease.
METHODS: All of the TOS with objective neurologic deficit treated in our unit 
between 1989 and 2011 were assessed retrospectively. Thirty cases were 
identified in 28 patients (two bilateral cases). The mean-age was 44 years (16 
to 70).
RESULTS: Muscular atrophy always predominated in the lateral thenar muscles. 
Seventeen also had sensory symptoms. Twenty-two patients (24 cases) were 
surgically treated. Twenty-three cases could be assessed with a mean follow-up 
of 39 months. Recovery was complete in four cases (17%), marked in nine cases 
(39%) and minimal in ten cases (44%).

distinguished from other types of neurological TOS. Muscular atrophy in the hand 
appears insidiously and the pain, which is inconstant, stays always in the 
background. Duration of symptoms before surgical treatment is the main 
prognostic factor.

OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study was to evaluate patient-reported long-term 
outcomes in patients with neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome (nTOS) and venous 
TOS (vTOS), who underwent first rib resection and anterior scalenectomy (FRRAS).
METHODS: Single institution, retrospective chart review from 2015 to 2025 was 
completed after obtaining institutional review board approval. Baseline 
demographic and clinical data were collected for patients who underwent surgery 
at least 1 year earlier. A five-question quality of life (QOL) survey was 
provided to patients through phone call or the electronic health record. 
Descriptive statistics including number (%) of categorical factors or median and 
interquartile range of continuous factors were reported. Differences between TOS 
subtypes were assessed using Fisher exact test (categorical) or rank-sum tests 
(continuous).
RESULTS: Of the 204 patients who underwent FRRAS, 104 completed our survey 
(57/114 nTOS and 47/90 vTOS). Patients with nTOS had significantly longer 
preoperative symptom duration (median [interquartile range], 24 [12-60] vs 2 
[1-10] months for vTOS; P < .001) with no other differences between groups. In 
nTOS, most patients (43/57, 75.4%) indicated improved QOL, regardless of the 
surgical approach. Although most patients did not have recurrent symptoms 
(32/57, 56.1%), those who did were more likely to be older (median age, 39 
[35-46] vs 27 [17-39] years; P = .003). 30/57 patients (52.6%) reported ongoing 
paresthesias, though 47/57 patients (82.5%) did not require chronic medications.

reoperative surgery (30% vs 4.3%; P = .033). Similarly, in vTOS, most patients 
(41/47, 87.2%) reported improved QOL, regardless of the surgical approach. Most 
veins (45/47, 95.7%) were patent at the time of follow-up and did not affect 
outcome. Younger patients were more likely to have improvement (median, 31 
[22-41] vs 47 [44-50] years; P = .015). Patients with recurrent symptoms, 
paresthesias, chronic medication use, or ongoing physical therapy/occupational 
therapy needs were significantly older (median age: 49 [43-53] vs 30 [21-39] 
years, P < .001; 42 [31-48] vs 30 [20-41] years, P = .027; 52 [50-55] vs 32 
[22-41] years, P = .007; and 43 [41-51] vs 31 [21-41] years, P = .014).
CONCLUSIONS: Patient-reported long-term outcomes are favorable for patients with 
nTOS and vTOS undergoing FRRAS. Our study highlights differences in long-term 
QOL by age, with younger patients having longer-term symptom-free experiences. 
Although a small proportion of patients have recurrent symptoms, most report 
improved QOL.

10. J Vasc Surg. 2010 Jun;51(6):1538-47. doi: 10.1016/j.jvs.2009.12.022. Epub

A comprehensive review of Paget-Schroetter syndrome.

Illig KA(1), Doyle AJ.

Medical Center, Rochester, NY 14642, USA. karl_illig@urmc.rochester.edu

Venous thoracic outlet syndrome progressing to the point of axilosubclavian vein 
thrombosis, variously referred to as Paget-Schroetter syndrome or effort 
thrombosis, is a classic example of an entity which if treated correctly has 
minimal long-term sequelae but if ignored is associated with significant 
long-term morbidity. The subclavian vein is highly vulnerable to injury as it 
passes by the junction of the first rib and clavicle in the anterior-most part 
of the thoracic outlet. In addition to extrinsic compression, repetitive forces 
in this area frequently lead to fixed intrinsic damage and extrinsic scar tissue 
formation. Once primary thrombosis is recognized, catheter-directed thrombolytic 
therapy is usually successful if initiated within ten to 14 days of clot 
formation, but often unmasks an underlying lesion. The vast majority of 
investigators believe that decompression of the venous thoracic outlet, usually 
by means of first rib excision, partial anterior scalenectomy, resection of the 
costoclavicular ligament, and thorough external venolysis, is necessary, 
although opinion is less uniform as to the need for and method of treatment of 
the venous lesion itself. Using this algorithm, long-term success rates of 95 to 
100% have been reported by many investigators. This review, in addition to 
discussing the overall treatment algorithm in more detail, attempts to point out 
controversies that still exist and research directions, both clinical and basic, 
that need to be pursued. Prospective randomized trials addressing this entity 
are surprisingly lacking, and although there is consensus based on experience, 
it may be necessary to step back and rigorously explore several aspects of this 
entity.

Early results of a highly selective algorithm for surgery on patients with 
neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome.

Chandra V(1), Olcott C 4th, Lee JT.

CA 94305, USA.

Comment in
    J Vasc Surg. 2011 Dec;54(6):1705. doi: 10.1016/j.jvs.2011.05.104.

OBJECTIVE: Neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome (nTOS) encompasses a wide 
spectrum of disabling symptoms that are often vague and difficult to diagnose 
and treat. We developed and prospectively analyzed a treatment algorithm for 
nTOS utilizing objective disability criteria, thoracic outlet syndrome 
(TOS)-specific physical therapy, radiographic evaluation of the thoracic outlet, 
and selective surgical decompression.
METHODS: Patients treated for nTOS from 2000-2009 were reviewed (n = 93). In 
period 1, most patients were offered surgery with documentation of appropriate 
symptoms. A prospective observational study began in 2007 (period 2) and was 
aimed at determining which patients benefited most from surgical intervention. 
Evaluation began with a validated mini-QuickDASH (QD) quality-of-life scale 
(0-100, 100 = worse) and duplex imaging of the thoracic outlet. Patients then 
participated in TOS-specific physical therapy (PT) for 2 to 4 months and were 
offered surgery based on response to PT and improvement in symptoms.
RESULTS: Thirty-four patients underwent first rib resection in period 1 (68% 
female, mean age 39, 18% athletes, 15% workers comp). In operated patients 
undergoing duplex imaging, 47% showed compression of their thoracic outlet 
arterial flow on provocative positioning. Based on subjective improvement of 
symptoms, 56% of patients at 1 year had a positive outcome. In period 2 during 
the prospective cohort, 59 consecutive patients were evaluated for nTOS (64% 
female, mean age 36, 32% athletes, 12% workers comp) with a mean pre-PT QD 
disability score of 55.1. All patients were prescribed PT, and 24 (41%) were 
eventually offered surgical decompression based on compliance with PT, interval 
improvement on QD score, and duplex compression of the thoracic outlet. 
Twenty-one patients underwent surgery (SURG group) consisting of first rib 
resection, middle and anterior scalenectomy, and brachial plexus neurolysis. 
There were significant differences between the SURG and non-SURG cohorts with 
respect to age, participation in competitive athletics, history of trauma, and 
symptom improvement with PT. At 1-year follow-up, 90% of patients expressed 
symptomatic improvement with the mean post-op QD disability score decreasing to 
24.9 (P = .005) and 1-year QD scores improving down to 20.5 (P = .014).
CONCLUSIONS: This highly-selective algorithm for nTOS surgery leads to 
improvement in overall success rates documented subjectively and objectively. 
Compliance with TOS-specific PT, improvement in QD scores after PT, young age, 
and competitive athletics are associated with improved surgical outcomes. 
Long-term follow-up will be necessary to document sustained symptom relief and 
to determine who the optimal surgical candidates are.

A comprehensive review of Paget-Schroetter syndrome.

Venous thoracic outlet syndrome progressing to the point of axilosubclavian vein 
thrombosis, variously referred to as Paget-Schroetter syndrome or effort 
thrombosis, is a classic example of an entity which if treated correctly has 
minimal long-term sequelae but if ignored is associated with significant 
long-term morbidity. The subclavian vein is highly vulnerable to injury as it 
passes by the junction of the first rib and clavicle in the anterior-most part 
of the thoracic outlet. In addition to extrinsic compression, repetitive forces 
in this area frequently lead to fixed intrinsic damage and extrinsic scar tissue 
formation. Once primary thrombosis is recognized, catheter-directed thrombolytic 
therapy is usually successful if initiated within ten to 14 days of clot 
formation, but often unmasks an underlying lesion. The vast majority of 
investigators believe that decompression of the venous thoracic outlet, usually 
by means of first rib excision, partial anterior scalenectomy, resection of the 
costoclavicular ligament, and thorough external venolysis, is necessary, 
although opinion is less uniform as to the need for and method of treatment of 
the venous lesion itself. Using this algorithm, long-term success rates of 95 to 
100% have been reported by many investigators. This review, in addition to 
discussing the overall treatment algorithm in more detail, attempts to point out 
controversies that still exist and research directions, both clinical and basic, 
that need to be pursued. Prospective randomized trials addressing this entity 
are surprisingly lacking, and although there is consensus based on experience, 
it may be necessary to step back and rigorously explore several aspects of this 
entity.

OBJECTIVE: Neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome (nTOS) encompasses a wide 
spectrum of disabling symptoms that are often vague and difficult to diagnose 
and treat. We developed and prospectively analyzed a treatment algorithm for 
nTOS utilizing objective disability criteria, thoracic outlet syndrome 
(TOS)-specific physical therapy, radiographic evaluation of the thoracic outlet, 
and selective surgical decompression.
METHODS: Patients treated for nTOS from 2000-2009 were reviewed (n = 93). In 
period 1, most patients were offered surgery with documentation of appropriate 
symptoms. A prospective observational study began in 2007 (period 2) and was 
aimed at determining which patients benefited most from surgical intervention. 
Evaluation began with a validated mini-QuickDASH (QD) quality-of-life scale 
(0-100, 100 = worse) and duplex imaging of the thoracic outlet. Patients then 
participated in TOS-specific physical therapy (PT) for 2 to 4 months and were 
offered surgery based on response to PT and improvement in symptoms.
RESULTS: Thirty-four patients underwent first rib resection in period 1 (68% 
female, mean age 39, 18% athletes, 15% workers comp). In operated patients 
undergoing duplex imaging, 47% showed compression of their thoracic outlet 
arterial flow on provocative positioning. Based on subjective improvement of 
symptoms, 56% of patients at 1 year had a positive outcome. In period 2 during 
the prospective cohort, 59 consecutive patients were evaluated for nTOS (64% 
female, mean age 36, 32% athletes, 12% workers comp) with a mean pre-PT QD 
disability score of 55.1. All patients were prescribed PT, and 24 (41%) were 
eventually offered surgical decompression based on compliance with PT, interval 
improvement on QD score, and duplex compression of the thoracic outlet.

resection, middle and anterior scalenectomy, and brachial plexus neurolysis. 
There were significant differences between the SURG and non-SURG cohorts with 
respect to age, participation in competitive athletics, history of trauma, and 
symptom improvement with PT. At 1-year follow-up, 90% of patients expressed 
symptomatic improvement with the mean post-op QD disability score decreasing to 
24.9 (P = .005) and 1-year QD scores improving down to 20.5 (P = .014).

improvement in overall success rates documented subjectively and objectively.

and competitive athletics are associated with improved surgical outcomes.

to determine who the optimal surgical candidates are.

"""One-page takeaways: TOS in pitchers, what to watch for and when to act.

Companion to TOS_CASE_REVIEW_ER_2026-10-07. Evidence only, no clinical
judgments. Sources: the 18 September 2026 TOS evidence review, plus nine
papers checked against PubMed (E-utilities) on 2026-10-07. No athlete names.
"""
import sys
from pathlib import Path

sys.path.insert(0, r"C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Baylor_Doc_Style")
from baylor_docstyle import BaylorDoc  # noqa: E402

OUT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]  # SpecialRequests/TOS_ES
STEM = "TOS_ONEPAGER_ER_2026-10-07"


def build():
    d = BaylorDoc(
        "TOS in Pitchers: What to Watch and When to Act",
        deck="Takeaways from the TOS case review for Athletic Medicine, "
             "Athletic Performance and softball staff.",
        status="Internal",
    )

    d.section("What to watch for")
    d.bullets([
        "**Medial elbow pain with ulnar-side symptoms** (ring and small "
        "finger numbness, forearm tightness). In all three of our cases this "
        "pointed the workup at the elbow first. TOS was recognised only after "
        "symptoms spread.",
        "**Spread beyond the elbow:** neck, chest or upper-trap pain, "
        "headaches, a heavy or dead arm, loss of control.",
        "**Vein or artery signs, which are urgent:** a swollen, full or "
        "blue-tinged hand or arm; cold, pale fingers.",
        "**Load dependence:** symptoms that rise with pitch volume or "
        "intensity, or with the arm overhead.",
    ])

    d.section("How fast to act")
    d.table(
        ["Situation", "Act", "What the research says"],
        [
            ["Sudden arm or hand swelling, or colour change",
             "Same day: ultrasound and vascular referral",
             "Clot-dissolving treatment works best within 10 to 14 days of "
             "the clot, and improves vein patency (Illig 2010; Chun 2022)"],
            ["Pitcher with elbow pain plus any symptom above",
             "Put TOS in the workup at the first visit and image then",
             "No study sets a deadline. Published algorithms image at the "
             "first TOS evaluation (Chandra 2011)"],
            ["Confirmed neurogenic TOS",
             "Supervised, measured PT trial. Scalene block during workup",
             "Trials of 6 weeks (Balderman 2019) to 2 to 4 months "
             "(Chandra 2011). Block response is a diagnostic criterion"],
            ["Not improving after the PT trial",
             "Get the surgical opinion. Do not let it drift",
             "Surgery within 3 months of diagnosis: chronic pain at 5 years "
             "14.5 vs 22.4 percent (Phuyal 2025, n=2,593)"],
        ],
        widths=[1.55, 1.95, 3.2],
        compact=True,
    )

    d.section("Recovery after surgery")
    d.para(
        "Athletes returned to competition at an average of **4.6 months** "
        "(Chandra 2014, n=41). Seventy percent returned to the same or "
        "better level, and half did so within a year (Shutze 2017, n=67, "
        "two thirds baseball or softball). Professional pitchers took **9 to "
        "11 months** (evidence review, section 1.6). For a pitcher returning "
        "to full workload, the long end of that range is the honest planning "
        "number."
    )

    d.section("Does recovery mirror how long symptoms lasted?")
    d.para(
        "**Not as a rule.** No study tests a one-for-one link between "
        "symptom duration and recovery time. The direction has some "
        "support. Patients with unresolved symptoms after surgery had "
        "longer symptom histories, 90 vs 48 months, though they were also "
        "older and more often smokers (Rochlin 2012). Earlier surgery was "
        "linked to less chronic pain (Phuyal 2025), and in TOS with nerve "
        "loss, duration was the main predictor of outcome (Marty 2012). One "
        "study found the opposite: shorter duration predicted worse results "
        "(Yavuzer 2004). Fair summary: long-standing symptoms make full "
        "resolution less likely. They do not set the recovery clock."
    )

    d.section("Three habits for every future case")
    d.numbered([
        "**Count every pitch**, bullpen and warm-up included.",
        "**Measure every two weeks:** QuickDASH, grip, key pinch, symptom "
        "log.",
        "**Write the decision dates down at diagnosis:** when the PT trial "
        "will be judged, and by whom.",
    ])

    d.small(
        "Sources, each checked against PubMed 2026-10-07: Illig 2010 PMID "
        "20304578; Chun 2022 PMID 35643200; Chandra 2011 PMID 21803527; "
        "Balderman 2019 PMID 30852035; Phuyal 2025 PMID 41151323; Chandra "
        "2014 PMID 24835692; Shutze 2017 PMID 28943009; Rochlin 2012 PMID "
        "22770848; Marty 2012 PMID 23067684; Yavuzer 2004 PMID 14747108. "
        "Eric Rash, Applied Performance, 7 October 2026."
    )

    path = OUT / f"{STEM}.docx"
    d.save(path)
    print(path)
    return path


if __name__ == "__main__":
    build()

RESULTS: A total of 60 patients (40.0% with VTOS and 60.0% with NTOS) were 
included. The average age of the VTOS patients was 17.2 years vs 16.6 years for 
the NTOS patients (P = .265). The NTOS patients were more likely to be female 
(88.9% vs 62.5%; P = .024). The NTOS patients had more frequently presented with 
pain (97.2% vs 70.8%; P = .005), paresthesia (94.4% vs 29.1%; P = .021), and 
weakness (67.7% vs 12.5%; P = .004) but had less often reported swelling (25.0% 
vs 95.8%; P < .001). At presentation, the NTOS patients had also reported a 
longer symptom duration (17.7 months vs 3.1 months; P < .001). Transaxillary 
first rib resection with subtotal scalenectomy was performed for 100% of the 
VTOS patients and 94.4% of the NTOS patients undergoing cervical rib resection 
(2.8%) or scalenectomy alone (2.8%). Additionally, 11.1% of the NTOS patients 
had undergone combined first rib resection and cervical rib resection. For the 
VTOS patients, postoperative venography showed patent subclavian veins in 27.8%. 
In addition, 44.4% had required venoplasty, 16.8% had required thrombolysis, and 
11% were chronically occluded. No significant differences were found in blood 
loss, operative time, or length of stay between the groups. No surgical 
complications occurred. The average follow-up was 6.3 months. Significant 
differences were found between the VTOS and NTOS groups for the pre- and 
postoperative somatic pain scale, QuickDASH, and Derkash scores. Complete 
symptom resolution had occurred in 83.3% of the VTOS and 75% of the NTOS 
patients (P = .074). No statistically significant difference in the return to 
sport was observed between the two groups (VTOS, 94.4%; vs NTOS, 73.9%; P = 
.123). Of the NTOS patients, 10.0% had had other concomitant injuries and 5.0% 
had had medical conditions that had precluded their return to sport. Logistic 
regression found no significant relationship between the preoperative somatic 
pain scale score, QuickDASH score, or duration of symptoms and the return to 
sport.
CONCLUSIONS: Adolescent athletes with VTOS and NTOS can have good functional 
between overhead athletes and nonathletes and investigate the return to 
same-level sports rate in overhead athletes.

content.text:
I've pushed the gitignore commit, built the one-page doc, and had Codex check every claim in both documents. I fixed everything it flagged, and both documents rebuilt cleanly: the one-pager at 1 page, the case review at 7.

**Your four questions, as the one-pager answers them:**
- **What to look out for:** medial elbow pain with ring- and small-finger symptoms; spread to the neck, chest, upper trap or head; a heavy or dead arm that gets worse with pitch volume or with the arm overhead. A swollen, full or blue-tinged hand, or cold, pale fingers, is urgent.
- **How quickly to image:**
  - Swelling or colour change: same day. Clot-dissolving treatment works best within 10–14 days of the clot forming.
  - Nerve-type TOS: no study sets a deadline. Published treatment pathways image at the first TOS evaluation.
- **How quickly to inject or operate:**
  - The published pathways start with a physical therapy (PT) trial lasting 6 weeks to 4 months.
  - A large matched study found surgery within 3 months of diagnosis left less chronic pain at 5 years: 14.5% vs 22.4%.
  - These two timelines will look like they conflict, and a physician will likely ask how they fit together.
- **Rehab time after surgery:** overhead athletes returned at 7.3 months on average, and 97% got back to sport. Professional pitchers took 9–11 months.

**Does recovery time mirror how long symptoms lasted?** No. The one study that tested this in athletes (60 adolescents) found no significant link between symptom duration and return to sport. Several studies in ordinary patients do link longer symptoms to worse final results, and one found the opposite. Long symptoms may make a full recovery less likely, but they don't set the recovery clock.

**What Codex found:** it checked 94 claims and 75 passed. Its three failures, all now fixed:
- **Wrong wording on workload:** the case review said no workload figure "appears anywhere", but Carrie's summary mentions the 15-inning game.
- **Wrong description of the duration studies:** the one-pager called them "non-athlete cohorts with symptoms measured in years". One of them timed surgery from diagnosis, not from when symptoms started.
- **Overstated lower-body claim:** "lower-body capacity explains half of shoulder load" overstated the source. Screening measures predicted about half of the difference between pitchers; nobody has tested whether conditioning lowers the load.

I also softened the claims it marked as stronger than the evidence:
- my chance estimate now reads "1.6–7.6%, hypothetical"
- the NCAA no-pitch-limit claim notes the rulebook still needs checking
- the "how fast to act" steps and the recommended actions are now labelled as proposals for Athletic Medicine and the physicians to confirm.

Two of its warnings concerned facts from Carrie's summary, which Codex didn't have. I had already checked those against her document myself.

**Before this goes out:**
- **Botox timing isn't in the one-pager.** No study I found sets a timeline for it. One surgical study found patients who had Botox before surgery were more likely to have unresolved symptoms afterward (46% vs 20%). That more likely marks harder cases than shows Botox causes anything. Adding it would mean cutting something else to stay on one page.
- **Shutze 2017 contradicts itself.** Its results say half returned within 1 year, while its conclusion says within 6 months. Dr. Pearl co-authored it, so I dropped the timing figure rather than pick one.
- **The case review and one-pager disagree on one point.** Section 3.1 of the review still says the evidence review doesn't test symptom duration as a predictor, which the one-pager now covers. If the two go out together, I can add a sentence pointing to the one-pager.
- **What went to Codex:** the one-pager went as written. The case review went redacted, with no names, initials, school or physicians, so nothing identifiable reached OpenAI.

Everything is in `TOS_ES`, which is gitignored, so there's nothing new to commit.

Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\closeout

# Closeout

One command that replaces the manual end-of-day sequence: "any loose ends?" → "commit and push what needs to be" → "is this in memory?" → "write a handoff so Codex can pick this up."

Run all five checks, then give ONE verdict. Do not ask permission between steps — the invocation of this skill IS the authorization for the full sequence. Commit and push is standing-authorized for every DEV repo: each repo's `AGENTS.md` Session routine says "update STATUS, commit, push at end", and unpushed work on one machine is the top cause of conflicts on the other. The only exceptions are repos whose `CLAUDE.md` says their data must stay local (DexaProject is the precedent); commit those locally and list them as open.

This one file serves Claude Code, Codex and Cowork (uploaded to claude.ai). Cowork has no TaskList and no Claude Code memory hooks: do what applies there and say what was skipped.

## Step 1 — Loose-ends sweep

- `git status` across **every** repo in DEV, not only the ones named in this conversation. Another session, another harness, or the other machine may have left work dirty, and a closeout that only checks what it remembers touching will say "clear to sign off" over someone else's uncommitted work. Walk `DEV/`, `DEV/Football/` and `DEV/SpecialRequests/`, and report any repo with uncommitted or unpushed commits. The full walk takes about 90 seconds.
  - Windows: `git -C <repo> status --porcelain` per repo. Do NOT use `Get-ChildItem -Recurse` to look for files; it silently skips paths past the 260-character limit. Inside a repo, `git ls-files` is the reliable way to ask whether a file exists.
  - Repos with dirty state you did not touch: commit and push them like any other, and name them in the report so the user knows another session left them.
- **Registry drift.** Run `python <dir of portfolio_json>/portfolio.py crosswalk` (`portfolio_json` is in `~/.claude/skills/_shared/config.<platform>.json`). It compares `portfolio.json` with every DEV folder and Drive `01_PROJECTS` folder and only reports; it never moves anything. Do not fix drift during closeout. List each item it found under "Still open", naming any folder created this session first: that is a project started without a row, the exact way projects got lost before the 2026-10-03 organization pass. `drive_unreachable` means the Drive checks never ran; say so, do not call it clean. Cowork cannot run it; say it was skipped.
- **7-day rule.** Run `python <dir of portfolio_json>/portfolio.py seven-day --apply`. Name any project it paused, and any project on its last two days, under "Still open" with what it still needs (a receiver, step 1). Revive with the board's status pill or `portfolio.py` once there is a first step to show.
- Unfinished todos/tasks from this session (TaskList if available).
- Background jobs or workflows still running.
- Anything the user was promised earlier in the session that wasn't delivered.

## Step 2 — Commit & push

- **Registry edits get their own commit.** In project-triage, if `git status --porcelain portfolio.json` shows a change (board edits from the day, `set-status`, `set-receiver`), commit that file alone first as `data: board edits <YYYY-MM-DD>`, then the rest. The board header's "N unpushed registry edits" counts these; a skipped one becomes a JSON merge conflict when the other machine edits too.
- Every repo touched this session: stage, commit with a descriptive message, `git pull --no-rebase` (the other machine may have pushed), push. If the merge conflicts, follow the conflict steps in `dev-sync/SKILL.md` (they are the one home for them), then push and list the file under "Still open".
- Before staging, make sure any new file over 95 MB and any `.env` is in `.gitignore`.
- Local-only repos (CLAUDE.md says so): commit, do not push, list it.
- If `~/.claude/mods` changed this session (a mod added, edited or `.disabled`), run the mods sync (`bash ~/.claude/mods/mods-sync.sh` on the Mac, `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File $HOME\.claude\mods\mods-sync.ps1` on Windows) and list any invalid mod under "Still open".
- Also check the three config repos, `~/.claude` (dotclaude), `~/.claude/skills` (claude-skills) and `~/.claude/global-memory` (claude-global-memory). If any has changes, commit and push it the same way, so the other machine's `/dev-sync` picks it up.
- **Push `global-memory` even on a light session.** `daily-backup` pushes it nightly, which is too late for a same-day handoff: work the Mac in the afternoon, sit down at Windows that evening, and anything written to MEMORY.md or handoffs is still only on the Mac. Pushing it here is what makes memory available to the other machine tonight rather than tomorrow. It is the only repo that carries memory across, so treat an unpushed `global-memory` the same as an unpushed project repo: it blocks "clear to sign off".
- Nothing to commit → say so in one line, move on.

## Step 3 — Memory verification

- Check `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log` — must be empty. If not, surface contents and fix the hook issue if obvious.
- Confirm today's transcript file exists at `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/<today>.md` and was modified within the last few hours. On a Cowork-only day it may be absent; say so, it is not an error.
- Run the dev-docs harvest so repo docs reach memsearch: `bash ~/.claude/scripts/harvest-dev-docs.sh` (Mac) or `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File $HOME\.claude\scripts\harvest-dev-docs.ps1` (Windows). It copies every repo's `docs/*.md` into `~/.claude/global-memory/dev-docs/`, which is on the index list. One line of output; do this after Step 4 so today's STATUS is included.
- If this session produced a durable decision or new active thread, update `~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md` (respect the 2,500-char cap; consolidate before adding) or write a Tier A memory file per the memory-system rules in CLAUDE.md.
- **Tier A does not cross machines — mirror it or lose it.** Project memory lives under a slug built from the project's absolute path, and that path differs on the Mac and the Windows laptop, so a Tier A file written today is not auto-injected tomorrow on the other machine. Global memory and the repo both cross; Tier A does not. So for every Tier A fact written this session, ask: is this durable and project-scoped? If yes, it must also land in the repo — `docs/STATUS.md` for current state, `docs/DECISIONS.md` for a decision and its reasoning, the dated handoff for the detail. Treat Tier A as a fast local cache and the repo as the record. If a fact only ever exists in Tier A, assume the other machine will never see it.

## Step 4 — Cross-harness handoff

This is the **canonical durable handoff** — the one future sessions and other harnesses read. (For a mid-session, chat-only summary before `/clear`, that's the `session-handoff` skill; the mattpocock `handoff` skill writes to the OS temp dir and is not durable — don't rely on it for cross-session state.)

If real work happened this session (not just Q&A), write a handoff to
`<repo>/docs/handoffs/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<slug>.md` (or `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/` if no repo fits):

- What was being worked on and why
- Decisions made (with the reasoning that would be lost)
- Exact file paths of everything created or modified this session
- Next actions, most important first
- Anything mid-flight (open questions, awaited inputs)

Plain markdown, no harness-specific syntax — Codex, Antigravity, or a fresh Claude session must be able to resume from it. Commit it with the Step 2 commit when in a repo.

**Always, in every repo touched (even for light sessions): update `docs/STATUS.md`.** It is the file the next session reads first, on either machine, in any harness. Rewrite the sections in place, keep it short:

- `## Current state` — two to five lines on where things stand today
- `## Next` — most important first. Item 1 is one concrete action (a command to run or a file to open), not a theme: it is the line `~/.claude/scripts/where-was-i.py` shows Eric the next morning
- `## Open questions` — decisions waiting on Eric, each one written out in full as its own top-level bullet: the question itself and enough context to answer it without opening another file. Never a pointer ("See PLAN.md"): `/startup` reads this section across every repo with `where-was-i.py --decisions`, and a pointer gives no question to answer. Mark answered items `ANSWERED <date>: …` or strike them through (`~~…~~`) so they drop off that list. Leave the section empty, not "-", when nothing is waiting.
- `## Gotchas` — anything that will bite the next session

Then run `python ~/.claude/scripts/where-was-i.py --decisions --days 1`. It prints exactly what tomorrow's `/startup` will show as "Decisions waiting on you". Every decision this session left open must appear there as a readable question; if one is missing or shows as a pointer, fix that repo's `## Open questions` before the commit.

The dated handoff file is the detailed record; STATUS.md is the summary. Do Step 4 before the Step 2 commit so both land in the same push.

**Keep the resume cards true (PM system design Decision 9).** The live board shows each project as a card read from STATUS and the registry; if a card doesn't make sense tonight, it won't in six weeks. Run `python <dir of portfolio_json>/landed.py scan --days 1` (about a minute), then `python <dir of portfolio_json>/portfolio.py card-check`. It prints the card of every registry project touched today, on either machine, with its gaps. Fix each gap before the Step 2 commit:

- `STATUS has no entry dated <today>`: add `- <today>: <what happened>` under the repo's Done / Current state.
- `STATUS has no Next item`: put one concrete action first under `## Next`.
- `no next step (next_action)` (Drive-only row): set it on the board or with `portfolio.py add-update <name> "<note>" --next-action "<step>"`.
- `needs a receiver`: `portfolio.py set-receiver <name> "<who>"` (a name, or `me: <why>`). Ask Eric when it is not obvious from the session; never invent one.
- `touched but marked <status>`: revive it (`portfolio.py set-status <name> active`) or say in STATUS why a retired project was touched.

Re-run `card-check` after the fixes. Its output is the last section of the report (**Cards:**); trim to projects with work today if it is long, but never drop one that still has a gap.

## Step 5 — Verdict

End with a single short report:

```
## Closeout — <date>

**Committed & pushed:** <repos + one-line summary, or "nothing to commit">
**STATUS.md:** updated in <repos>
**Memory:** captured ✓ / issue found: <what> / skipped (Cowork, no hooks)
**Handoff:** <path, or "not needed — no substantive work">
**Registry drift:** <N items, or "none"> (`portfolio.py crosswalk`)
**Still open:** <numbered list, or "none">

Clear to sign off. / Not clear: <the one thing blocking>.

**Cards:** <`portfolio.py card-check` output, after the Step 4 fixes>
```

The cards come last on purpose: they are what the next session, on either machine, picks up from.

"Clear to sign off" means: every touched repo is pushed (or is a declared local-only repo). If anything is unpushed, the verdict is "Not clear" and the unpushed repo is the one thing blocking.

Every file created or modified during the session must appear somewhere in the report with its full path — "where did this save?" should never need to be asked.

**Where everything landed.** Build that list from the ledger, not from memory: the Step 4 `landed.py scan --days 1` already refreshed it (it reads git in every DEV repo and file times on Drive and the vault, so files written by scripts and shell copies are included); run `landed.py show --days 1`. Put its project-grouped output in the report under **Landed:** (trim to the projects this session touched if it is long). The ledger lives in `~/.claude/global-memory/landed/` and is pushed with global-memory, so `/landed` on the other machine shows it too.

## Rules

- Push every touched DEV repo. Do not leave the laptop with unpushed work; the other machine pulls from GitHub, not from this disk.
- Never skip Step 3 — memory capture failing silently is the user's top recurring worry.
- If a check fails and the fix is quick and safe (restage a file, clear a stale lock), fix it and note it. If the fix is risky, list it under "Still open" instead.
- Total output should fit on one screen. The user is leaving; brevity is the deliverable.

# Handoff 2026-10-07: TOS case review and staff one-pager

No athlete names here on purpose. Case details live only in `SpecialRequests/TOS_ES/`
(gitignored) and on Drive.

## What was done and why
Athletic Medicine wrote an executive summary of three softball pitchers with thoracic
outlet syndrome (two operated, one in nonoperative care). Eric asked for an expert,
objective review of it, using this repo's September evidence brief. Then he asked for a
one-page staff handout on what to watch for, how fast to act, and rehab expectations,
plus a check of the claim "recovery takes as long as the symptoms lasted".

## Outputs (all outside this repo)
- `SpecialRequests/TOS_ES/TOS_CASE_REVIEW_ER_2026-10-07.docx` and `.pdf` (7 pages)
- `SpecialRequests/TOS_ES/TOS_ONEPAGER_ER_2026-10-07.docx` and `.pdf` (1 page)
- Build scripts: `SpecialRequests/TOS_ES/scripts/build_tos_case_review.py` and `build_tos_onepager.py`
- Drive copy of everything, including the source summary:
  `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\04_RESEARCH\TOS_Case_Review_2026-10\`
- `SpecialRequests/.gitignore`: `TOS_ES/` added (commit e3d851f, pushed)

## Decisions
- Eric does not put his name on clinical judgments. Both documents cite evidence only. Where
  evidence runs out they ask the treating physicians a question, and clinical steps are
  labelled proposals for Athletic Medicine to confirm.
- Cases appear by number and initials only. Nothing identifiable went to an external
  service. Codex got a redacted copy of the review.
- Codex fact-check: 94 claims checked, 75 passed, 3 failed. All fails and most warnings were
  fixed, including the chance estimate (now "at least three: 1.6 to 7.6 percent, hypothetical").

## Findings worth keeping
- This brief's point 2 is wrong as written (see STATUS Next).
- "Recovery mirrors symptom duration" is not supported. The one athlete study that tested
  duration against return to sport found no significant association (Talutis 2023,
  PMID 36243264). Several general-patient studies link longer symptoms to worse final
  outcomes (Rochlin 2012, 22770848; Phuyal 2025, 41151323; Marty 2012, 23067684). One found
  the opposite (Yavuzer 2004, 14747108).
- Timing sources: Illig 2010 (20304578) and Chun 2022 (35643200) on venous clots, where
  thrombolysis works best within 10 to 14 days of the clot forming. PT trial lengths come
  from Balderman 2019 (30852035, 6 weeks) and Chandra 2011 (21803527, 2 to 4 months). Early
  surgery means within 3 months of diagnosis (Phuyal 2025).
- Return to play after rib resection: Funakoshi 2024 (38707577), 7.3 months on average,
  97 percent returned. Shutze 2017 (28943009, co-author Dr. Pearl, Baylor Scott & White)
  contradicts itself: its results say half returned within 1 year, its conclusion says
  within 6 months.
- Preoperative Botox was more common among patients left with unresolved symptoms
  (Rochlin 2012: 46 vs 20 percent). That is a marker, not a cause. It is not in the
  one-pager.

## Next
1. Fix point 2 in both brief documents (STATUS Next).
2. Eric decides on distribution of case review section 8 (SpecialRequests STATUS).
3. Optionally point case review section 3.1 to the one-pager's duration evidence.

- Cases appear by number and initials only. Nothing identifiable went to an external
  service. Codex got a redacted copy of the review.
- Codex fact-check: 94 claims checked, 75 passed, 3 failed. All fails and most warnings were
  fixed, including the chance estimate (now "at least three: 1.6 to 7.6 percent, hypothetical").

## Findings worth keeping
- This brief's point 2 is wrong as written (see STATUS Next).
- "Recovery mirrors symptom duration" is not supported. The one athlete study that tested
  duration against return to sport found no significant association (Talutis 2023,
  PMID 36243264). Several general-patient studies link longer symptoms to worse final
  outcomes (Rochlin 2012, 22770848; Phuyal 2025, 41151323; Marty 2012, 23067684). One found
  the opposite (Yavuzer 2004, 14747108).
- Timing sources: Illig 2010 (20304578) and Chun 2022 (35643200) on venous clots, where
  thrombolysis works best within 10 to 14 days of the clot forming. PT trial lengths come
  from Balderman 2019 (30852035, 6 weeks) and Chandra 2011 (21803527, 2 to 4 months). Early
  surgery means within 3 months of diagnosis (Phuyal 2025).
- Return to play after rib resection: Funakoshi 2024 (38707577), 7.3 months on average,
  97 percent returned. Shutze 2017 (28943009, co-author Dr. Pearl, Baylor Scott & White)
  contradicts itself: its results say half returned within 1 year, its conclusion says
  within 6 months.
- Preoperative Botox was more common among patients left with unresolved symptoms
  (Rochlin 2012: 46 vs 20 percent). That is a marker, not a cause. It is not in the
  one-pager.

## Next
1. Fix point 2 in both brief documents (STATUS Next).
2. Eric decides on distribution of case review section 8 (SpecialRequests STATUS).
3. Optionally point case review section 3.1 to the one-pager's duration evidence.
